title: Acute coronary syndromes
summary: Diagnosis, risk stratification and UK-guideline management of STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina, including antiplatelet strategy and secondary prevention.
content:
## Overview

Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) share a common pathology: rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombus. The spectrum runs from unstable angina (ischaemia without myocardial necrosis) through non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) to ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), which usually reflects complete coronary occlusion. MRCP Part 1 questions focus on ECG interpretation, troponin kinetics, the choice of reperfusion strategy and the evidence base for secondary prevention.

## Classification

| Syndrome | ECG | Troponin | Typical pathology |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unstable angina | Normal, ST depression or T inversion | Normal | Partial occlusion, no necrosis |
| NSTEMI | ST depression, T inversion or normal | Raised | Partial or transient occlusion |
| STEMI | ST elevation or new LBBB | Raised | Complete occlusion |

Fourth Universal Definition criteria: a rise and/or fall of high-sensitivity troponin with at least one value above the 99th centile, plus symptoms, ECG change, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium, or angiographic thrombus.

## ECG territories

- Anterior: V1-V4, left anterior descending artery
- Lateral: I, aVL, V5-V6, circumflex
- Inferior: II, III, aVF, right coronary artery in about 80 percent
- Posterior: ST depression V1-V3 with tall R waves; confirm with V7-V9
- Right ventricular infarction accompanies inferior STEMI; look for ST elevation in V4R and avoid nitrates if hypotensive

## Immediate management

- Aspirin 300 mg loading dose for all patients unless truly contraindicated
- Oxygen only if saturations fall below 94 percent (hyperoxia is harmful)
- Morphine and antiemetic for ongoing pain; glyceryl trinitrate if not hypotensive
- STEMI: primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given, and within 12 hours of symptom onset. Otherwise fibrinolysis (for example tenecteplase) followed by transfer for angiography
- Second antiplatelet: prasugrel is preferred with primary PCI (clopidogrel if on an oral anticoagulant); ticagrelor or clopidogrel for NSTEMI
- Anticoagulation: unfractionated heparin with bivalirudin or heparin alone during PCI; fondaparinux for NSTEMI not undergoing immediate angiography

## Risk stratification in NSTEMI

The GRACE score predicts six-month mortality and guides timing of angiography. Patients at intermediate or higher risk (predicted mortality above 3 percent) should have coronary angiography within 72 hours; unstable patients need it immediately. Low-risk patients may be managed conservatively with ischaemia testing.

## Complications

- Arrhythmia: ventricular fibrillation is the leading cause of pre-hospital death; complete heart block is common with inferior infarction and often resolves
- Mechanical: papillary muscle rupture (acute mitral regurgitation, day 2-7), ventricular septal rupture (pansystolic murmur, step-up in oxygen saturation), free wall rupture (tamponade)
- Left ventricular thrombus and mural aneurysm (persistent ST elevation)
- Dressler syndrome: pericarditis two to ten weeks post infarct, treated with NSAIDs or colchicine

## Secondary prevention

All patients should leave hospital on aspirin indefinitely, a second antiplatelet for 12 months, high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker. Add an aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone) if there is heart failure with an ejection fraction of 40 percent or less. Cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation and glycaemic and blood pressure control complete the package.

## Key points

- Troponin rise and fall plus clinical context defines infarction; a single raised value is not diagnostic
- Primary PCI within 120 minutes is the reperfusion strategy of choice for STEMI
- GRACE score guides timing of angiography in NSTEMI
- Avoid nitrates in right ventricular infarction and oxygen in normoxic patients
- Dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months, then aspirin alone
- Eplerenone improves survival post-MI when ejection fraction is 40 percent or below

title: Atrial fibrillation
summary: Classification, stroke risk assessment with CHA2DS2-VASc, rate versus rhythm control and anticoagulation choices in atrial fibrillation.
content:
## Overview

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, affecting around 2 percent of adults in the UK and rising steeply with age. It is characterised by chaotic atrial electrical activity with an irregularly irregular ventricular response and absence of P waves. The clinical priorities are symptom control, prevention of thromboembolic stroke and treatment of the underlying cause.

## Classification

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| First diagnosed | First detected episode regardless of duration |
| Paroxysmal | Self-terminating, usually within 48 hours, always within 7 days |
| Persistent | Lasts more than 7 days or requires cardioversion |
| Long-standing persistent | Continuous for more than 12 months |
| Permanent | Accepted; no further attempts at rhythm control |

## Causes

Cardiac: hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, mitral valve disease, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, pericarditis. Non-cardiac: thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, electrolyte disturbance, obstructive sleep apnoea. Lone AF occurs without structural disease. Check thyroid function, electrolytes and an echocardiogram in every new diagnosis.

## Haemodynamically unstable patients

Shock, syncope, acute heart failure or ongoing ischaemia mandate emergency synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of duration of AF. Give heparin at the same time.

## Rate control

Rate control is the default first-line strategy for most patients. Options are a standard beta-blocker (not sotalol), a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil, avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction) or digoxin. Digoxin monotherapy is acceptable only in sedentary patients or those with heart failure. Combine two agents if one is insufficient; never combine a beta-blocker with verapamil.

## Rhythm control

Consider rhythm control when there is a reversible cause, new-onset AF, heart failure thought to be caused by AF, or when rate control fails to relieve symptoms. Cardioversion may be electrical or pharmacological (flecainide or amiodarone; flecainide only with a structurally normal heart). If AF has lasted more than 48 hours, anticoagulate for at least three weeks first or exclude left atrial thrombus with transoesophageal echocardiography. Long-term rhythm maintenance uses beta-blockers, dronedarone, flecainide, sotalol or amiodarone. Catheter ablation of the pulmonary veins is offered when drugs fail or are not tolerated.

## Stroke prevention

Use CHA2DS2-VASc to estimate risk: Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age 75 or over (2 points), Diabetes, prior Stroke or TIA (2 points), Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Sex category female. Offer anticoagulation to men with a score of 1 or more and women with a score of 2 or more, after assessing bleeding risk with ORBIT. A high bleeding score is a prompt to modify risk factors, not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) are first line. Warfarin is reserved for moderate to severe mitral stenosis, mechanical valves or when DOACs are contraindicated. Aspirin has no role in stroke prevention in AF. Left atrial appendage occlusion is an option when anticoagulation is contraindicated.

## Special situations

- Wolff-Parkinson-White with AF: avoid AV nodal blockers (adenosine, digoxin, verapamil, beta-blockers); use flecainide or DC cardioversion
- After stroke: start anticoagulation after two weeks in disabling stroke, immediately after TIA
- Post-operative AF is often self-limiting but still warrants anticoagulation assessment

## Key points

- Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves; always look for precipitants and check thyroid function
- Unstable patients need immediate DC cardioversion
- Rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem is first line for most
- Anticoagulate men scoring 1 or more and women scoring 2 or more on CHA2DS2-VASc
- DOACs are preferred over warfarin unless there is a mechanical valve or significant mitral stenosis
- Avoid AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF

title: Cytochrome P450 drug interactions
summary: The key enzyme inducers and inhibitors, their clinical consequences and the drugs with narrow therapeutic windows most affected.
content:
## Overview

The cytochrome P450 (CYP) system is a family of hepatic microsomal enzymes responsible for phase I oxidative metabolism of most lipophilic drugs. Isoenzymes CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP1A2 account for the majority of clinically relevant interactions. Enzyme induction increases metabolism and reduces drug levels; inhibition does the reverse. Interactions matter most for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index such as warfarin, phenytoin, ciclosporin, theophylline and the combined oral contraceptive.

## Enzyme inducers

Induction requires synthesis of new enzyme, so the effect takes days to weeks to develop and to wear off after the inducer is withdrawn.

| Inducer | Notes |
|---|---|
| Phenytoin | Also auto-induces its own metabolism |
| Carbamazepine | Reduces efficacy of contraceptives and warfarin |
| Rifampicin | Most potent clinical inducer; also induces P-glycoprotein |
| Barbiturates (phenobarbital) | |
| St John's Wort | Over-the-counter; reduces ciclosporin, HIV protease inhibitor and contraceptive levels |
| Chronic alcohol excess | Induces CYP2E1 |
| Smoking | Induces CYP1A2; theophylline and clozapine doses fall on cessation |
| Griseofulvin | |

A useful mnemonic is PC BRAS: Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Barbiturates, Rifampicin, Alcohol (chronic), Sulphonylureas, or alternatively CRAP GPS with Griseofulvin, Phenobarbital and St John's Wort added.

## Enzyme inhibitors

Inhibition is usually rapid in onset because it depends only on the inhibitor reaching adequate concentrations.

| Inhibitor | Notes |
|---|---|
| Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin) | Azithromycin is a weaker inhibitor |
| Azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole, itraconazole) | |
| Ciprofloxacin | Inhibits CYP1A2; raises theophylline |
| Amiodarone | Long half-life so inhibition persists for weeks |
| Sodium valproate | |
| Isoniazid | |
| SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine, fluvoxamine) | Inhibit CYP2D6; reduce tamoxifen activation |
| Omeprazole | CYP2C19; may reduce clopidogrel activation |
| Ritonavir and cobicistat | Deliberately used to boost other antiretrovirals |
| Grapefruit juice | Inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 |
| Acute alcohol intake | |
| Allopurinol | Inhibits xanthine oxidase rather than CYP; raises azathioprine toxicity |

Mnemonic SICKFACES.COM: Sodium valproate, Isoniazid, Cimetidine, Ketoconazole, Fluconazole, Alcohol (acute), Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin, Sulphonamides, Ciprofloxacin, Omeprazole, Metronidazole.

## Prodrugs behave in reverse

Clopidogrel, codeine and tamoxifen require CYP activation. Inhibitors reduce their effect: fluoxetine with tamoxifen and omeprazole with clopidogrel are classic examples. Poor metaboliser CYP2D6 genotypes (around 7 percent of Europeans) gain little analgesia from codeine, whereas ultra-rapid metabolisers risk opioid toxicity.

## Clinically important scenarios

- Warfarin: INR rises with macrolides, azoles, amiodarone and metronidazole; falls with rifampicin, carbamazepine and St John's Wort
- Combined oral contraceptive: failure with rifampicin, rifabutin and enzyme-inducing antiepileptics; non-inducing antiepileptics such as lamotrigine (with caveats), levetiracetam and sodium valproate are safe
- Statins: simvastatin and atorvastatin levels rise dangerously with clarithromycin, itraconazole and grapefruit; pravastatin and rosuvastatin are less affected
- Theophylline: toxicity precipitated by ciprofloxacin, erythromycin and smoking cessation
- Ciclosporin and tacrolimus: levels fall with rifampicin and rise with azoles and diltiazem

## Key points

- Inducers act over days to weeks; inhibitors act within hours to days
- Rifampicin is the most potent inducer; macrolides, azoles and amiodarone are the most frequently examined inhibitors
- Prodrugs such as clopidogrel, codeine and tamoxifen are less effective with CYP inhibition
- Smoking induces CYP1A2, so theophylline and clozapine levels rise on cessation
- Always check INR within days of starting or stopping an interacting drug in a warfarinised patient

title: Management of common poisonings
summary: Recognition and treatment of paracetamol, salicylate, tricyclic, opioid, benzodiazepine, lithium and digoxin toxicity with an emphasis on UK protocols.
content:
## Overview

Poisoning accounts for a large share of acute medical admissions in the UK. The MRCP Part 1 examiner expects you to match toxidromes to agents, know the threshold for antidotes and recognise the situations in which enhanced elimination is indicated. TOXBASE and the National Poisons Information Service underpin UK practice.

## General principles

- Activated charcoal 50 g within one hour of ingestion for most agents; ineffective for iron, lithium, alcohols, acids and alkalis
- Whole bowel irrigation for iron and sustained-release preparations
- Urinary alkalinisation for salicylates
- Haemodialysis for lithium, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, metformin lactic acidosis and severe theophylline toxicity (mnemonic: I STUMBLE - isopropanol, salicylate, theophylline, uraemia, methanol, barbiturates, lithium, ethylene glycol)

## Paracetamol

Hepatotoxicity results from saturation of glucuronidation and sulphation with accumulation of NAPQI once glutathione is depleted. Take a level at 4 hours or later and plot against the single UK treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours). Start acetylcysteine immediately if ingestion is staggered, the timing is uncertain, presentation is beyond 8 hours with a significant ingestion (over 150 mg/kg), or the patient is already symptomatic. The SNAP regimen delivers acetylcysteine over 12 hours with fewer anaphylactoid reactions than the traditional 21-hour regimen. King's College criteria for transplant referral: arterial pH below 7.3 after resuscitation, or all of INR above 6.5 (PT above 100 seconds), creatinine above 300 micromol/L and grade III-IV encephalopathy.

## Salicylates

Features: tinnitus, sweating, hyperventilation, vomiting, and a mixed respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis. Hypoglycaemia and hyperthermia indicate severe toxicity. Treat with charcoal, aggressive fluids and urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate. Haemodialysis for levels above 700 mg/L, renal failure, pulmonary oedema, seizures or refractory acidosis.

## Tricyclic antidepressants

Anticholinergic signs (dilated pupils, dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia), drowsiness, seizures and cardiotoxicity through sodium channel blockade. The ECG shows QRS widening (over 100 ms predicts seizures, over 160 ms predicts arrhythmia), a terminal R wave in aVR and QT prolongation. Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, hypotension or arrhythmia. Avoid class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics; lidocaine is the rescue agent for ventricular arrhythmia.

## Opioids and benzodiazepines

Opioid toxicity: pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, reduced conscious level. Naloxone 400 micrograms titrated intravenously; its half-life is shorter than most opioids, so an infusion is often needed. Benzodiazepine overdose is rarely fatal alone; flumazenil is reserved for iatrogenic sedation and avoided in mixed overdose or epilepsy because of seizure risk.

## Lithium

Toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides. Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Levels above 1.5 mmol/L are toxic; haemodialysis for severe neurological features or levels above 4 mmol/L in chronic toxicity. Charcoal does not bind lithium.

## Digoxin

Nausea, xanthopsia (yellow-green visual haloes), confusion and almost any arrhythmia; classic ECG findings are reverse tick ST depression and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Hypokalaemia potentiates toxicity. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab) are indicated for life-threatening arrhythmia, potassium above 6 mmol/L or serum levels above 15 nmol/L.

## Other antidotes

| Poison | Antidote |
|---|---|
| Beta-blocker | Glucagon, high-dose insulin |
| Calcium channel blocker | Calcium, high-dose insulin euglycaemia |
| Methanol, ethylene glycol | Fomepizole (or ethanol), haemodialysis |
| Organophosphate | Atropine, pralidoxime |
| Iron | Desferrioxamine |
| Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin, dicobalt edetate |
| Carbon monoxide | High-flow oxygen |
| Methaemoglobinaemia | Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) |

## Key points

- Treat paracetamol overdose above the 100 mg/L 4-hour line; start acetylcysteine immediately for staggered or late presentations
- Salicylate poisoning gives a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis; alkalinise urine and dialyse if severe
- QRS widening in tricyclic overdose is treated with sodium bicarbonate
- Lithium and salicylate are dialysable; charcoal does not bind lithium
- Hypokalaemia worsens digoxin toxicity and hyperkalaemia signals severity

title: Statistics for the MRCP: diagnostic tests and trial interpretation
summary: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, relative and absolute risk, number needed to treat and the common statistical tests used in clinical research.
content:
## Overview

Clinical Sciences contributes 25 questions to each Part 1 sitting and statistics is one of its most predictable components. Questions are almost always numerical and rely on constructing a two-by-two table quickly and accurately.

## Two-by-two table

| | Disease present | Disease absent |
|---|---|---|
| Test positive | True positive (TP) | False positive (FP) |
| Test negative | False negative (FN) | True negative (TN) |

- Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): proportion of diseased patients correctly identified. A highly sensitive test is useful for ruling out disease (SnNOut)
- Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): proportion of healthy people correctly identified. A highly specific test rules in disease (SpPIn)
- Positive predictive value = TP / (TP + FP): probability that a positive result is true; rises with prevalence
- Negative predictive value = TN / (TN + FN): falls as prevalence rises
- Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and are independent of prevalence; predictive values are not

## Likelihood ratios

- Positive likelihood ratio = sensitivity / (1 - specificity)
- Negative likelihood ratio = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity
- Post-test odds = pre-test odds multiplied by likelihood ratio
- A positive LR above 10 or a negative LR below 0.1 changes management meaningfully

## Measures of treatment effect

Suppose the event rate is 20 percent in the control group and 15 percent with treatment.

- Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = 0.20 - 0.15 = 0.05
- Relative risk (RR) = 0.15 / 0.20 = 0.75
- Relative risk reduction = 1 - RR = 25 percent
- Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / ARR = 20
- Odds ratio = (a/b) / (c/d) using the two-by-two table; approximates RR when events are rare
- Hazard ratio is the ratio of instantaneous event rates from survival analysis (Cox regression)

Number needed to harm is calculated identically from the absolute risk increase.

## Choosing a statistical test

| Data type | Two groups, unpaired | Two groups, paired | More than two groups |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parametric (normal continuous) | Unpaired t-test | Paired t-test | ANOVA |
| Non-parametric (ordinal or skewed) | Mann-Whitney U | Wilcoxon signed-rank | Kruskal-Wallis |
| Categorical | Chi-squared or Fisher exact | McNemar test | Chi-squared |

Correlation between two continuous variables uses Pearson (parametric) or Spearman (non-parametric). Regression predicts one variable from others.

## Distributions and error

- Normal distribution: mean equals median equals mode; 68 percent of values lie within one standard deviation, 95 percent within 1.96 and 99.7 percent within three
- Standard error of the mean = SD / square root of n; the 95 percent confidence interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 SE
- Type I error (alpha): rejecting a true null hypothesis, a false positive; conventionally set at 0.05
- Type II error (beta): failing to reject a false null hypothesis; power = 1 - beta, usually set at 80 or 90 percent
- Power increases with sample size, larger effect size and less variance
- Positively skewed data have mean greater than median; negatively skewed data the reverse

## Study designs and bias

Randomised controlled trials sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy for interventions, with intention-to-treat analysis preserving randomisation. Cohort studies yield relative risks; case-control studies yield odds ratios and are suited to rare diseases. Lead-time bias and length-time bias inflate the apparent benefit of screening. Funnel plots in meta-analysis reveal publication bias; the I-squared statistic measures heterogeneity.

## Key points

- Sensitivity and specificity are independent of prevalence; predictive values are not
- NNT = 1 / ARR; always use absolute, not relative, differences
- Use parametric tests for normally distributed data and non-parametric alternatives otherwise
- Power is 1 minus the type II error rate and is increased by a larger sample
- Case-control studies produce odds ratios; cohort studies produce relative risks
- A 95 percent confidence interval crossing 1 for a ratio (or 0 for a difference) means the result is not statistically significant

title: Patterns of genetic inheritance
summary: Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance with the classic conditions, pedigree clues and concepts such as anticipation and imprinting.
content:
## Overview

Genetics questions in Part 1 test pattern recognition: from a pedigree or a short description you must identify the mode of inheritance, calculate a risk for offspring, or recall which disorder follows which pattern. Learn the lists, then learn the exceptions.

## Autosomal dominant

One mutant allele suffices. Affected individuals appear in every generation, males and females are affected equally, and each child of an affected parent has a 50 percent risk. Many conditions are structural or involve receptors, and penetrance may be incomplete.

Examples: adult polycystic kidney disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia, Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, tuberous sclerosis, myotonic dystrophy, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, von Willebrand disease (most types), familial adenomatous polyposis, Lynch syndrome, hereditary spherocytosis, achondroplasia, Ehlers-Danlos (most types), osteogenesis imperfecta, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, acute intermittent porphyria, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, MEN types 1 and 2.

## Autosomal recessive

Both alleles must be mutated. Affected individuals usually have unaffected carrier parents, siblings are affected in a horizontal pattern, and consanguinity increases risk. Most are enzyme deficiencies or metabolic disorders. Two carrier parents have a 25 percent chance of an affected child, a 50 percent chance of a carrier and a 25 percent chance of an unaffected non-carrier. An unaffected sibling of an affected child has a two-thirds chance of being a carrier.

Examples: cystic fibrosis (CFTR, delta F508), sickle cell disease, beta thalassaemia, haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y), Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, phenylketonuria, glycogen storage diseases, Friedreich ataxia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Gilbert syndrome, homocystinuria, Fanconi anaemia, ataxia telangiectasia.

## X-linked recessive

Males are affected; females are usually carriers and unaffected (or mildly affected through skewed X-inactivation). There is no male-to-male transmission: an affected father passes the gene to all his daughters and none of his sons. A carrier mother has a 50 percent chance of an affected son and a 50 percent chance of a carrier daughter.

Examples: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, haemophilia A and B, G6PD deficiency, Fabry disease, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, red-green colour blindness, X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, Alport syndrome (85 percent), androgen insensitivity, Hunter syndrome, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

## X-linked dominant

Both sexes affected but females more commonly; affected fathers transmit to all daughters and no sons. Examples: vitamin D-resistant (hypophosphataemic) rickets, Rett syndrome, fragile X (with unusual features), Alport syndrome in some families.

## Mitochondrial inheritance

Transmitted exclusively through the maternal line because sperm contribute no mitochondria. Affected mothers pass the condition to all children; affected fathers to none. Heteroplasmy produces variable expression. Examples: MELAS, MERRF, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, Leigh syndrome.

## Trinucleotide repeat disorders and anticipation

Expansion of the repeat in successive generations produces earlier onset and greater severity (anticipation).

| Disorder | Repeat | Inheritance |
|---|---|---|
| Huntington disease | CAG | Autosomal dominant |
| Myotonic dystrophy | CTG | Autosomal dominant |
| Fragile X | CGG | X-linked |
| Friedreich ataxia | GAA | Autosomal recessive |
| Spinocerebellar ataxias | CAG | Autosomal dominant |

## Imprinting and other concepts

Genomic imprinting: Prader-Willi (loss of paternal 15q11-13) and Angelman (loss of maternal copy) arise from the same region. Uniparental disomy is an alternative mechanism. Mosaicism explains variable severity in conditions such as Turner syndrome. Penetrance is the proportion of genotype carriers who show the phenotype; expressivity describes variability of the phenotype among those affected. Homozygous dominant conditions such as familial hypercholesterolaemia are far more severe than heterozygous.

## Key points

- Dominant conditions are typically structural; recessive conditions are typically enzymatic
- No male-to-male transmission is the hallmark of X-linked inheritance
- Mitochondrial disorders are transmitted only by mothers
- Unaffected siblings of a recessive proband have a two-thirds carrier risk
- Anticipation is a feature of trinucleotide repeat expansion
- Prader-Willi and Angelman illustrate imprinting at chromosome 15

title: Psoriasis
summary: Clinical variants, triggers, associations and the stepwise topical, phototherapy, systemic and biologic management of psoriasis.
content:
## Overview

Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease affecting around 2 percent of the UK population. The pathology is a T-cell driven hyperproliferation of keratinocytes with a shortened epidermal turnover time, mediated by the IL-23 and IL-17 axis and TNF-alpha. Genetic susceptibility is strong (HLA-Cw6, PSORS1). Onset peaks in the late teens to twenties and again in the fifties.

## Clinical variants

| Variant | Features |
|---|---|
| Chronic plaque | Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, sacrum |
| Guttate | Raindrop lesions on the trunk 2-4 weeks after streptococcal throat infection; often resolves in 3 months |
| Flexural (inverse) | Smooth, shiny, non-scaly plaques in axillae, groin, submammary folds |
| Pustular | Palmoplantar pustulosis (linked to smoking) or generalised pustular psoriasis (a medical emergency) |
| Erythrodermic | Over 90 percent body surface involvement; risk of hypothermia, dehydration and sepsis |
| Nail | Pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil-drop discolouration |

Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed. Koebner phenomenon describes new lesions at sites of trauma.

## Triggers

- Drugs: beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids
- Streptococcal infection (guttate), HIV
- Trauma, stress, alcohol, smoking, obesity
- Sunlight usually helps but can occasionally provoke

## Associations

- Psoriatic arthritis in up to 30 percent, including symmetrical polyarthritis, asymmetrical oligoarthritis, distal interphalangeal disease, spondyloarthritis and arthritis mutilans
- Metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- Inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis
- Depression and reduced quality of life; assess with DLQI

## Management

**First line topical therapy** for chronic plaque disease: a potent corticosteroid applied once daily plus a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) once daily, applied at different times, for up to 4 weeks. If inadequate, vitamin D analogue twice daily alone, then potent steroid twice daily or a coal tar preparation. Limit potent steroids to 8 weeks and very potent to 4 weeks at any one site, with a 4-week steroid-free break between courses. Scalp: potent steroid; face and flexures: mild or moderate steroid or calcineurin inhibitor. Emollients throughout.

**Phototherapy**: narrowband UVB three times weekly is the next step for extensive disease. PUVA (psoralen plus UVA) is more effective but carries a higher skin cancer risk.

**Systemic non-biologic**: methotrexate is first choice (weekly dosing with folic acid; monitor FBC, LFTs and renal function; teratogenic). Ciclosporin is preferred when rapid control is needed or conception is planned. Acitretin is a retinoid useful for pustular disease but highly teratogenic with a three-year post-treatment contraception requirement. Apremilast (PDE4 inhibitor) and dimethyl fumarate are alternatives.

**Biologics** are indicated when PASI is 10 or more and DLQI is over 10 despite standard systemic therapy: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-12/23 inhibitor (ustekinumab), IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) and IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab). Screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis before starting.

## Key points

- Silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp and sacrum with nail changes is classic
- Beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarials and steroid withdrawal are the key drug triggers
- Guttate psoriasis follows streptococcal infection and usually self-resolves
- First-line topical therapy is a potent steroid plus a vitamin D analogue
- Methotrexate is first-line systemic therapy; biologics target TNF, IL-17 or IL-23
- Screen for psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic risk at every review

title: Skin cancers: basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma
summary: Risk factors, clinical recognition, precursor lesions and management principles for the three common skin malignancies, including melanoma staging and referral criteria.
content:
## Overview

Skin cancer is the most common malignancy in the UK. Ultraviolet exposure is the dominant risk factor for all three major types, but their behaviour differs greatly: basal cell carcinoma almost never metastasises, squamous cell carcinoma has a modest metastatic potential, and melanoma is responsible for the majority of skin cancer deaths.

## Shared risk factors

- Cumulative or intermittent UV exposure, sunburn in childhood, sunbed use
- Fair skin (Fitzpatrick types I and II), red hair, freckling
- Immunosuppression, particularly after solid organ transplantation (SCC risk rises up to 100-fold)
- Ionising radiation, arsenic exposure, chronic scars and ulcers (Marjolin ulcer for SCC)
- Genetic syndromes: xeroderma pigmentosum, Gorlin syndrome (multiple BCCs), familial atypical mole syndrome

## Basal cell carcinoma

The most common skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes, typically on sun-exposed head and neck in older adults. Nodular BCC is a pearly, translucent papule with rolled edges, surface telangiectasia and often central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Superficial BCC appears as a scaly erythematous plaque on the trunk; morphoeic BCC is an ill-defined scar-like plaque with a higher recurrence rate. Growth is slow and local; metastasis is exceptionally rare. Refer routinely rather than urgently unless there is concern about delay. Treatment is surgical excision with a 4 mm margin; Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk or facial lesions; alternatives include curettage, cryotherapy, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy and radiotherapy. Vismodegib (hedgehog pathway inhibitor) is used for locally advanced or metastatic disease.

## Squamous cell carcinoma

Arises from suprabasal keratinocytes and presents as an indurated, keratotic or ulcerated nodule that grows over weeks to months, often on the ears, lips, scalp or dorsum of hands. Precursor lesions are actinic keratoses (rough scaly patches on sun-damaged skin treated with cryotherapy, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod or diclofenac gel) and Bowen disease (SCC in situ, a well-defined red scaly plaque, often on the lower leg). Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing, self-resolving lesion that is difficult to distinguish clinically and is usually excised. High-risk features for metastasis: diameter over 2 cm, depth over 4 mm, poor differentiation, perineural invasion, ear or lip site, immunosuppression. Excise with 4 mm margins (6 mm for high-risk). Refer suspected SCC on a two-week-wait pathway.

## Melanoma

Malignant proliferation of melanocytes. Subtypes: superficial spreading (most common, younger adults, trunk and legs), nodular (most aggressive, rapidly growing dome-shaped lesion), lentigo maligna (face of the elderly, slow radial growth), acral lentiginous (palms, soles, nail beds; most common type in darker skin) and amelanotic.

Assess pigmented lesions with the ABCDE rule (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution) and the weighted seven-point checklist, in which change in size, shape or colour score two points each and diameter over 7 mm, inflammation, oozing or altered sensation score one each. Refer urgently if the score is 3 or more.

Breslow thickness is the single most important prognostic factor; ulceration and mitotic rate also matter. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered for lesions over 0.8 mm or with ulceration.

| Breslow thickness | Excision margin |
|---|---|
| In situ | 5 mm |
| Up to 1 mm | 1 cm |
| 1-2 mm | 1-2 cm |
| Over 2 mm | 2 cm |

Adjuvant and metastatic treatment has been transformed by immune checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, ipilimumab) and, for the 40-50 percent with BRAF V600 mutations, combined BRAF and MEK inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib).

## Key points

- BCC: pearly, rolled edge, telangiectasia; local destruction, virtually never metastasises
- SCC: keratotic or ulcerated nodule arising from actinic keratosis or Bowen disease; transplant patients are at very high risk
- Melanoma: ABCDE and the seven-point checklist; refer urgently if score 3 or more
- Breslow thickness is the key prognostic factor and dictates excision margin
- BRAF V600 mutation status guides targeted therapy in advanced melanoma
- Checkpoint inhibitors have markedly improved survival in metastatic melanoma

title: Thyroid disorders: hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism
summary: Causes, interpretation of thyroid function tests and UK management of hyper- and hypothyroidism, including Graves disease, thyroiditis, thyroid storm and myxoedema coma.
content:
## Overview

Thyroid disease is common, affects women five to ten times more often than men, and is heavily represented in Part 1. Questions typically present a set of thyroid function tests and ask for the cause or the next step in treatment.

## Interpreting thyroid function tests

| TSH | Free T4 | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Low | High | Primary hyperthyroidism |
| Low | Normal | Subclinical hyperthyroidism or T3 toxicosis (check T3) |
| High | Low | Primary hypothyroidism |
| High | Normal | Subclinical hypothyroidism |
| Low or normal | Low | Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid |
| High or normal | High | TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance |

Amiodarone, lithium, interferon and immune checkpoint inhibitors commonly disturb thyroid function. Biotin supplements interfere with immunoassays.

## Hyperthyroidism: causes

- Graves disease (75 percent): TSH receptor stimulating antibodies; diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema and thyroid acropachy are specific to Graves
- Toxic multinodular goitre: older patients, patchy uptake on scintigraphy
- Toxic adenoma: single hot nodule
- Thyroiditis (subacute de Quervain, postpartum, silent, drug-induced): transient thyrotoxicosis with low uptake, often followed by hypothyroidism; raised ESR and painful gland in de Quervain
- Exogenous thyroxine, struma ovarii, gestational trophoblastic disease

## Hyperthyroidism: management

- Beta-blockade (propranolol) for symptom control while definitive treatment takes effect
- Carbimazole is first-line antithyroid drug: either titration to euthyroidism or block-and-replace with levothyroxine, for 12 to 18 months in Graves disease; agranulocytosis is the feared idiosyncratic reaction, so patients must report sore throat or fever. Carbimazole is teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia), so propylthiouracil is used in early pregnancy before switching back
- Radioactive iodine is first-line definitive treatment in the UK for Graves disease and nodular disease unless contraindicated (pregnancy, breastfeeding, active thyroid eye disease, young children). Most patients become hypothyroid
- Thyroidectomy for large compressive goitre, patient preference or failed medical therapy
- Thyroid eye disease: stop smoking, selenium for mild disease, high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for moderate to severe active disease; teprotumumab is a newer IGF-1 receptor antagonist

Thyroid storm presents with fever, tachyarrhythmia, delirium and heart failure; treat with propranolol, propylthiouracil (or carbimazole), Lugol's iodine given at least an hour after antithyroid drugs, hydrocortisone and supportive care.

## Hypothyroidism: causes

- Hashimoto thyroiditis: anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, firm goitre, associated with other autoimmune disease and a small increased risk of thyroid lymphoma
- Atrophic autoimmune thyroiditis, iodine deficiency worldwide
- Iatrogenic: post radioiodine, surgery, amiodarone, lithium
- Secondary: pituitary disease; TSH is unreliable, so monitor free T4 and replace cortisol before thyroxine

## Hypothyroidism: management

Levothyroxine 1.6 micrograms/kg daily for young healthy adults; start at 25 to 50 micrograms and titrate in the elderly or those with ischaemic heart disease. Check TSH 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, aiming for the reference range. Increase the dose by 25 to 50 micrograms as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors impair absorption. Treat subclinical hypothyroidism if TSH is above 10 mU/L on two occasions, or if symptomatic, pregnant or planning pregnancy with TSH above the reference range.

Myxoedema coma: hypothermia, bradycardia, hyponatraemia, reduced consciousness; treat with intravenous liothyronine or levothyroxine, hydrocortisone and slow rewarming.

## Key points

- Low TSH with high T4 is primary hyperthyroidism; Graves is distinguished by eye disease, pretibial myxoedema and TSH receptor antibodies
- Carbimazole causes agranulocytosis; propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester
- Radioiodine is first-line definitive therapy for Graves disease in the UK but is contraindicated in active eye disease
- Thyroiditis causes transient hyperthyroidism with low radioiodine uptake
- Treat subclinical hypothyroidism when TSH exceeds 10 mU/L
- In secondary hypothyroidism, replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine

title: Adrenal disorders: Addison disease and Cushing syndrome
summary: Causes, biochemical diagnosis and management of adrenal insufficiency and glucocorticoid excess, including dynamic tests and sick day rules.
content:
## Overview

The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (zona fasciculata), mineralocorticoids (zona glomerulosa) and androgens (zona reticularis). Deficiency and excess of cortisol are both examined heavily, with an emphasis on selecting the correct dynamic test and interpreting the results.

## Adrenal insufficiency

**Primary (Addison disease)**: destruction of the whole cortex, so both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient and ACTH is high. Autoimmune adrenalitis (anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies) accounts for 80 percent in the UK; tuberculosis is the leading cause worldwide. Other causes: adrenal metastases, haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome in meningococcal sepsis, anticoagulation), adrenoleukodystrophy, HIV, antiphospholipid syndrome.

**Secondary**: pituitary or hypothalamic disease, or suppression by exogenous steroids. Aldosterone is preserved because the renin-angiotensin system is intact, so hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation are absent.

Clinical features: fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, postural hypotension, salt craving, nausea, abdominal pain, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases and buccal mucosa (ACTH cross-reacting at melanocortin receptors), vitiligo. Biochemistry: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, mild hypercalcaemia, normocytic anaemia, eosinophilia.

Diagnosis: 9 am cortisol below 100 nmol/L is highly suggestive; above 400 nmol/L usually excludes. Confirm with the short Synacthen test (250 micrograms tetracosactide): a 30-minute cortisol below 420-450 nmol/L (assay-dependent) is abnormal. A raised ACTH with raised renin confirms primary disease.

Management: hydrocortisone 15-25 mg daily in divided doses (larger dose in the morning) plus fludrocortisone 50-200 micrograms. Patients need a steroid card, emergency injection kit and sick day rules: double the dose for fever or intercurrent illness and give intramuscular hydrocortisone if vomiting. Adrenal crisis presents with shock, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia; give 100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone immediately, then fluids and 200 mg over 24 hours.

## Cushing syndrome

Chronic glucocorticoid excess. Exogenous steroids are by far the commonest cause. Endogenous causes:

| Cause | Proportion | ACTH |
|---|---|---|
| Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) | 70 percent | High |
| Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid) | 10 percent | Very high |
| Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma | 20 percent | Low |

Features: central obesity, moon face, dorsocervical fat pad, purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, thin skin, hypertension, glucose intolerance, osteoporosis, depression, hirsutism and amenorrhoea. Hypokalaemic alkalosis and rapid onset with pigmentation suggest ectopic ACTH.

**Screening**: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol fails to suppress below 50 nmol/L), 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol. Two abnormal tests are required. Pseudo-Cushing states (alcohol, depression, obesity) can cause false positives.

**Localisation**: measure ACTH. If suppressed, image the adrenals. If detectable, perform a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (pituitary tumours partially suppress; ectopic sources do not) and pituitary MRI. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation distinguishes pituitary from ectopic disease when imaging is equivocal.

**Treatment**: trans-sphenoidal surgery for Cushing disease; adrenalectomy for adrenal tumours; resection of the ectopic source where possible. Metyrapone, ketoconazole and osilodrostat block cortisol synthesis while awaiting definitive treatment. Nelson syndrome (pituitary enlargement and pigmentation) may follow bilateral adrenalectomy.

## Key points

- Primary adrenal failure causes hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation; secondary does not
- Short Synacthen test is the diagnostic test of choice; treat with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone
- Double steroid doses during illness and give intramuscular hydrocortisone if vomiting
- Exogenous steroids are the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome; pituitary adenoma is the commonest endogenous cause
- Screen with overnight dexamethasone suppression, urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol
- Hypokalaemia and rapid onset point to ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer

title: Inflammatory bowel disease
summary: Distinguishing Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis, extra-intestinal manifestations, severity assessment and NICE-based induction and maintenance therapy.
content:
## Overview

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) comprises Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, chronic relapsing inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract driven by a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens in genetically susceptible individuals. Peak onset is 15-35 years with a second smaller peak in the sixties. Smoking worsens Crohn disease but protects against ulcerative colitis.

## Crohn disease versus ulcerative colitis

| Feature | Crohn disease | Ulcerative colitis |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Mouth to anus, terminal ileum commonest, skip lesions | Rectum extending proximally, continuous |
| Depth | Transmural | Mucosa and submucosa only |
| Histology | Non-caseating granulomas, goblet cells preserved | Crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion, no granulomas |
| Endoscopy | Cobblestoning, deep serpiginous ulcers, strictures | Diffuse erythema, friability, pseudopolyps, loss of vascular pattern |
| Complications | Fistulae, abscesses, strictures, perianal disease, malabsorption, gallstones, renal stones | Toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer, primary sclerosing cholangitis |
| Bleeding | Less common | Bloody diarrhoea typical |
| Smoking | Worsens | Protective |
| Surgery | Not curative; recurrence common | Colectomy is curative |

## Extra-intestinal manifestations

Related to disease activity: pauciarticular peripheral arthritis, erythema nodosum, episcleritis, aphthous ulcers. Unrelated to activity: axial spondyloarthritis, uveitis, pyoderma gangrenosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis (strongly associated with UC; check for cholestatic LFTs and perform MRCP). Osteoporosis, venous thromboembolism and anaemia (iron deficiency, B12 in ileal disease) are common.

## Investigations

Faecal calprotectin discriminates IBD from irritable bowel syndrome. Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are essential in every flare. Colonoscopy with biopsies is the diagnostic standard; avoid full colonoscopy in severe acute colitis because of perforation risk (flexible sigmoidoscopy instead). MR enterography or capsule endoscopy assesses small bowel Crohn disease. Abdominal X-ray in acute severe colitis looks for colonic dilatation over 6 cm.

## Assessing severity of ulcerative colitis

Truelove and Witts criteria define severe disease: six or more bloody stools daily plus at least one of temperature above 37.8, pulse above 90, haemoglobin below 105 g/L or ESR above 30 (CRP above 30).

## Management of ulcerative colitis

- Mild to moderate proctitis or left-sided disease: topical mesalazine (aminosalicylate), adding oral mesalazine, then topical or oral corticosteroid if no response within 4 weeks
- Extensive disease: high-dose oral mesalazine with topical treatment; oral prednisolone if inadequate
- Acute severe colitis: admit, intravenous hydrocortisone, low molecular weight heparin, avoid antimotility drugs and opioids. Assess at day 3: if stool frequency exceeds 8 or CRP is above 45 (Travis criteria), add rescue intravenous ciclosporin or infliximab and involve surgeons
- Maintenance: mesalazine first line; azathioprine or mercaptopurine after two or more flares needing steroids; biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, filgotinib, upadacitinib) or S1P modulators for refractory disease

## Management of Crohn disease

- Induction: glucocorticoids (prednisolone or budesonide for ileocaecal disease); exclusive enteral nutrition is an alternative, particularly in children; mesalazine is less effective than in UC
- Maintenance: azathioprine or mercaptopurine (check TPMT activity first), methotrexate if these are not tolerated; anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab), vedolizumab, ustekinumab or risankizumab for severe or fistulating disease
- Perianal fistulae: MRI, examination under anaesthesia, seton drainage, metronidazole or ciprofloxacin, anti-TNF
- Stop smoking; strictures may need resection or stricturoplasty; aim for bowel-sparing surgery

## Surveillance

Colonoscopic surveillance for colorectal cancer begins 10 years after onset of colitis, with intervals of 1, 3 or 5 years depending on risk; annually if PSC is present.

## Key points

- Crohn disease is transmural with skip lesions and granulomas; UC is continuous mucosal disease from the rectum
- Smoking worsens Crohn disease but is protective in UC
- Always exclude infection, including C. difficile, in an acute flare
- Truelove and Witts criteria define acute severe UC; rescue with ciclosporin or infliximab if no response by day 3
- Check TPMT before starting azathioprine or mercaptopurine
- Primary sclerosing cholangitis is linked to UC and mandates annual colonoscopy

title: Cirrhosis and its complications
summary: Causes and scoring of chronic liver disease, and the management of ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome.
content:
## Overview

Cirrhosis is the end result of chronic hepatic injury: diffuse fibrosis with nodular regeneration that disrupts hepatic architecture, raises portal pressure and impairs synthetic and detoxifying function. Alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and chronic viral hepatitis account for most UK cases; autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, haemochromatosis, Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency make up the remainder.

## Assessment

Compensated cirrhosis may be silent. Decompensation is marked by ascites, jaundice, variceal bleeding or encephalopathy. Examination findings include spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren contracture, caput medusae, splenomegaly and leuconychia.

| Child-Pugh parameter | 1 point | 2 points | 3 points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bilirubin (micromol/L) | Under 34 | 34-50 | Over 50 |
| Albumin (g/L) | Over 35 | 28-35 | Under 28 |
| INR | Under 1.7 | 1.7-2.3 | Over 2.3 |
| Ascites | None | Mild | Moderate to severe |
| Encephalopathy | None | Grade 1-2 | Grade 3-4 |

Class A (5-6), B (7-9) and C (10-15) predict one-year survival of roughly 100, 80 and 45 percent respectively. The MELD score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, sodium) is used for transplant prioritisation; UKELD is the UK equivalent. Transient elastography (FibroScan) quantifies fibrosis non-invasively.

## Ascites

Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) above 11 g/L indicates portal hypertension. Management: restrict sodium to under 5-6.5 g daily, spironolactone first line with furosemide added as needed, therapeutic paracentesis with albumin replacement (8 g per litre removed) for tense ascites, and consider transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) for refractory cases. Give prophylactic ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin when ascitic protein is below 15 g/L. Avoid NSAIDs.

## Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3 is diagnostic; the organism is most commonly Escherichia coli. Treat with intravenous cefotaxime or piperacillin-tazobactam plus intravenous albumin, which reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis after the first episode.

## Variceal bleeding

Resuscitate, then give terlipressin and broad-spectrum antibiotics before endoscopy, which should occur within 12 hours. Endoscopic band ligation is the treatment for oesophageal varices; injection of cyanoacrylate glue for gastric varices. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube or TIPSS is used for uncontrolled bleeding. Secondary prophylaxis combines a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol) with repeated banding. Primary prophylaxis with carvedilol is offered for medium or large varices.

## Hepatic encephalopathy

Ammonia and other neurotoxins bypass the liver. Grades run from subtle attention deficit and reversed sleep pattern (grade 1) through confusion and asterixis to coma (grade 4). Look for precipitants: infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, dehydration and TIPSS. Treat with lactulose aiming for two to three soft stools daily, and add rifaximin for secondary prevention.

## Hepatorenal syndrome

Functional renal failure from intense renal vasoconstriction in advanced cirrhosis. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes and lack of response to two days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin. Treat with terlipressin and albumin; liver transplantation is definitive.

## Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance

Six-monthly ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein for all patients with cirrhosis and for those with chronic hepatitis B at increased risk.

## Key points

- Child-Pugh uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy; MELD adds creatinine and sodium
- Spironolactone is the first-line diuretic for ascites; replace albumin after large-volume paracentesis
- Ascitic neutrophils above 250/mm3 confirm SBP; give cefotaxime and albumin
- Terlipressin and antibiotics before endoscopy in variceal haemorrhage; band ligation is definitive
- Lactulose first, then rifaximin, for hepatic encephalopathy; always seek a precipitant
- Six-monthly ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in all cirrhotics

title: Delirium
summary: Recognition, precipitants, screening tools and management of acute confusional state in older adults, and how to distinguish it from dementia and depression.
content:
## Overview

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with an additional change in cognition that is not better explained by pre-existing dementia. It affects 20-30 percent of older medical inpatients and up to 50 percent after hip fracture surgery. It is associated with longer stays, institutionalisation, accelerated cognitive decline and doubled mortality, yet it is missed in around two-thirds of cases, particularly the hypoactive form.

## Subtypes

- Hyperactive: agitation, restlessness, hallucinations, wandering, aggression
- Hypoactive: withdrawn, drowsy, quiet, reduced oral intake; the commonest and most frequently missed
- Mixed: fluctuating between the two

## Risk factors

Predisposing: age over 65, dementia or cognitive impairment, sensory impairment, frailty, polypharmacy, previous delirium, alcohol excess, depression. Precipitating: infection (urinary, respiratory), drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids, dopaminergic agents), drug or alcohol withdrawal, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance (sodium, calcium), hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, surgery, change of environment, sleep deprivation and hip fracture. Think PINCH ME: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment.

## Diagnosis

The 4AT is the recommended rapid screening tool in UK hospitals: Alertness, AMT4 (age, date of birth, place, current year), Attention (months of the year backwards) and Acute change or fluctuating course. A score of 4 or more suggests delirium. The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires acute onset with fluctuating course and inattention, plus either disorganised thinking or altered level of consciousness.

| Feature | Delirium | Dementia | Depression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Onset | Hours to days | Months to years | Weeks |
| Course | Fluctuating, worse at night | Progressive | Diurnal variation |
| Attention | Markedly impaired | Relatively preserved early | Poor concentration |
| Consciousness | Altered | Normal until late | Normal |
| Hallucinations | Common, visual | Later, in Lewy body dementia early | Rare, mood-congruent |
| Reversibility | Usually | No | With treatment |

Dementia with Lewy bodies can mimic delirium with fluctuation and visual hallucinations; a longer history and parkinsonism point towards it.

## Investigations

Bloods (FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, LFTs, CRP, TFTs, B12 and folate if not recently checked), urinalysis interpreted cautiously (asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and dipstick should not be used alone in the over-65s), chest X-ray, ECG, blood cultures if febrile. CT head if there is focal neurology, head injury, anticoagulation, or no cause is found. Medication review is mandatory, including recent cessation of alcohol or benzodiazepines.

## Management

Treat the cause and remove precipitants. Non-pharmacological measures are the foundation: reorientation with clocks and calendars, glasses and hearing aids, consistent staff, family presence, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, adequate hydration and nutrition, avoiding catheters and ward moves. Prevention strategies such as the Hospital Elder Life Program reduce incidence by around a third.

Pharmacological treatment is reserved for patients who are a danger to themselves or others or whose distress cannot be relieved otherwise. Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally or intramuscularly is first line, avoided in Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and QT prolongation, where a low dose of lorazepam or quetiapine is preferred. Benzodiazepines are otherwise avoided except for alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and increase stroke risk in dementia.

Post-delirium, patients should be reviewed for underlying dementia after recovery, since delirium unmasks cognitive impairment, and informed that they experienced a delirium episode.

## Key points

- Acute onset, fluctuating course and inattention are the core diagnostic features
- Hypoactive delirium is the commonest and most frequently missed form
- Screen with the 4AT; a score of 4 or more indicates probable delirium
- Do not diagnose urinary infection from dipstick alone in older adults
- Non-pharmacological reorientation and treatment of the cause are the mainstay
- Haloperidol is first line if sedation is essential, but is contraindicated in parkinsonism and Lewy body dementia

title: Falls and osteoporosis in older adults
summary: Multifactorial falls assessment, fracture risk estimation with FRAX and DXA, and the pharmacological and non-pharmacological management of osteoporosis.
content:
## Overview

Around a third of people over 65 and half of those over 80 fall each year. Falls are the leading cause of injury-related death in older adults and, combined with osteoporosis, produce more than 500,000 fragility fractures annually in the UK. Hip fracture carries a 30-day mortality of about 7 percent and one-year mortality approaching 30 percent, so falls and bone health should be assessed together.

## Multifactorial falls assessment

NICE recommends that any older person who presents with a fall, reports recurrent falls or shows gait or balance impairment should have a multifactorial assessment covering:

- Falls history, including circumstances, syncope or presyncope, and injuries
- Gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength (Timed Up and Go, Turn 180 test)
- Osteoporosis risk
- Cognitive assessment and mood
- Visual impairment
- Urinary incontinence
- Cardiovascular examination including lying and standing blood pressure (a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes is orthostatic hypotension)
- Home hazards
- Medication review

Culprit drugs: sedatives and hypnotics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihypertensives (especially alpha-blockers), diuretics, opioids, anticholinergics, hypoglycaemic agents and alcohol.

Interventions with proven benefit are strength and balance training, home hazard modification by an occupational therapist, medication reduction, cataract surgery, correction of visual impairment, treatment of postural hypotension and pacing for cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity.

## Osteoporosis

Defined by a bone mineral density T-score of -2.5 or lower on DXA at the hip or spine; osteopenia is a T-score between -1 and -2.5. Fragility fracture at the hip or vertebra establishes the diagnosis clinically regardless of DXA.

Risk factors: age, female sex, previous fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, glucocorticoid use (7.5 mg prednisolone or more for over 3 months), rheumatoid arthritis, low BMI, smoking, alcohol over 3 units daily, premature menopause, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, coeliac disease, chronic kidney disease, aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy, proton pump inhibitors, anticonvulsants, SSRIs and thiazolidinediones.

## Assessing fracture risk

Use FRAX or QFracture in women over 65, men over 75 and younger adults with risk factors. FRAX generates a 10-year probability of major osteoporotic fracture and hip fracture; the NOGG thresholds indicate whether to reassure, measure DXA or treat. Start treatment without DXA in patients aged 75 or over with a fragility fracture, and in those starting long-term high-dose glucocorticoids. Check calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D, renal and thyroid function, myeloma screen and testosterone in men to exclude secondary causes.

## Treatment

| Drug | Notes |
|---|---|
| Alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly | First line; take fasting, upright, with water, 30 minutes before food; contraindicated if eGFR below 35; oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures |
| Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously yearly | For intolerance or poor adherence; acute phase reaction after first dose |
| Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six-monthly | Anti-RANKL antibody; usable in renal impairment; rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without follow-on bisphosphonate; hypocalcaemia |
| Teriparatide | Recombinant PTH, anabolic, daily injection for 24 months; severe disease with vertebral fractures |
| Romosozumab | Anti-sclerostin, anabolic; avoid after MI or stroke |
| Raloxifene | Selective oestrogen receptor modulator; reduces vertebral fractures; raises VTE risk |
| HRT | Women under 60 with menopausal symptoms |

Correct vitamin D deficiency (loading followed by 800 IU daily) and ensure calcium intake of around 700-1200 mg daily before starting antiresorptives. Review bisphosphonates after 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous therapy; a drug holiday is reasonable if the T-score is above -2.5 and there have been no fractures.

## Key points

- Any older person who falls needs a multifactorial assessment including lying and standing blood pressure and medication review
- Strength and balance training is the single most effective falls intervention
- Osteoporosis is a T-score of -2.5 or below or a fragility fracture of hip or spine
- Use FRAX to decide who needs DXA and treatment; treat directly after fragility fracture at 75 or over
- Alendronate is first line; denosumab is an option in renal impairment but must not be stopped abruptly
- Always replace vitamin D and calcium before antiresorptive therapy

title: Approach to anaemia
summary: A structured approach to anaemia by mean cell volume, with the key laboratory discriminators for iron deficiency, thalassaemia, B12 and folate deficiency, haemolysis and anaemia of chronic disease.
content:
## Overview

Anaemia is a haemoglobin below 130 g/L in men and below 120 g/L in non-pregnant women (110 g/L in pregnancy). The mean cell volume (MCV) is the most useful first discriminator, followed by the reticulocyte count, which separates reduced production from increased destruction or loss. Part 1 questions rely on interpreting the blood film and a handful of iron and haemolysis studies.

## Microcytic anaemia (MCV below 80 fL)

| Cause | Ferritin | Serum iron | TIBC or transferrin | Other clues |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Iron deficiency | Low | Low | High | Pencil cells, raised platelets, low transferrin saturation |
| Anaemia of chronic disease | Normal or high | Low | Low | Raised CRP and ESR; may be normocytic |
| Thalassaemia trait | Normal | Normal | Normal | Very low MCV out of proportion to anaemia, raised red cell count, target cells |
| Sideroblastic anaemia | High | High | Low | Ring sideroblasts, basophilic stippling; lead, alcohol, isoniazid, myelodysplasia |
| Lead poisoning | Normal | Normal | Normal | Basophilic stippling, abdominal pain, neuropathy |

Ferritin is an acute phase protein; a level below 30 micrograms/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency but a normal value in an inflamed patient does not exclude it. The Mentzer index (MCV divided by red cell count) below 13 suggests thalassaemia, above 13 suggests iron deficiency. Any man or postmenopausal woman with iron deficiency needs upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation and coeliac serology. Treat with oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg once daily or on alternate days for three months after normalisation of haemoglobin; expect a rise of about 20 g/L every 3-4 weeks.

## Normocytic anaemia (MCV 80-100 fL)

Acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, chronic kidney disease (reduced erythropoietin), bone marrow failure, mixed deficiency, haemolysis, hypothyroidism and pregnancy. A raised reticulocyte count indicates a marrow response to haemorrhage or haemolysis; a low count implies hypoproliferation.

## Macrocytic anaemia (MCV above 100 fL)

**Megaloblastic** (hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes, impaired DNA synthesis):
- Vitamin B12 deficiency: pernicious anaemia (anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, associated autoimmune disease), gastrectomy, terminal ileal disease, metformin, proton pump inhibitors, vegan diet, nitrous oxide abuse. Neurological features include peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord (dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts). Treat with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, alternate days for two weeks if neurological involvement, then every 2-3 months for life
- Folate deficiency: poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, haemolysis, methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim. Always replace B12 before folate to avoid precipitating cord degeneration

**Non-megaloblastic**: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, drugs (azathioprine, hydroxycarbamide, zidovudine), aplastic anaemia, myeloma.

## Haemolytic anaemia

Markers: raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin, raised urinary urobilinogen. Haemoglobinuria and haemosiderinuria indicate intravascular haemolysis.

- Inherited: hereditary spherocytosis (autosomal dominant, spherocytes, positive EMA binding test, splenectomy curative), G6PD deficiency (X-linked, bite cells and Heinz bodies after oxidative stress from fava beans, primaquine, sulphonamides, dapsone), sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, pyruvate kinase deficiency
- Acquired immune: warm autoimmune haemolysis (IgG, spherocytes, direct antiglobulin test positive; idiopathic, lymphoma, CLL, SLE, methyldopa; treat with steroids and rituximab); cold agglutinin disease (IgM, complement, Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma; keep warm)
- Acquired non-immune: microangiopathic haemolysis with schistocytes (TTP, HUS, DIC, HELLP, malignant hypertension), paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (CD55 and CD59 deficiency, flow cytometry, eculizumab), mechanical heart valves, malaria, drugs

## Key points

- Classify by MCV, then use the reticulocyte count to distinguish underproduction from destruction or loss
- Low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency; normal ferritin does not exclude it during inflammation
- Investigate the gastrointestinal tract in all men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency
- Hypersegmented neutrophils signal megaloblastic anaemia; give B12 before folate
- Raised LDH and bilirubin with low haptoglobin indicate haemolysis; a positive DAT points to an immune cause
- Schistocytes on the film demand urgent exclusion of TTP and DIC

title: Leukaemias and lymphomas
summary: Distinguishing features, diagnostic markers and first-line management of acute and chronic leukaemias, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including key cytogenetic abnormalities.
content:
## Overview

Haematological malignancies are diagnosed by a combination of blood film, immunophenotyping, cytogenetics and molecular studies. Part 1 questions usually offer an age, a blood count pattern and a distinguishing feature such as a translocation, a specific cell on the film or a characteristic complication. Learn the discriminators.

## Acute leukaemias

Acute leukaemia is defined by more than 20 percent blasts in the marrow. Presentation is with marrow failure: anaemia, infection from neutropenia and bleeding from thrombocytopenia, usually over days to weeks.

**Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)** is the commonest acute leukaemia in adults. Auer rods are pathognomonic. Risk factors include prior chemotherapy, radiation, myelodysplasia, Down syndrome and benzene. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (t(15;17), PML-RARA) presents with disseminated intravascular coagulation and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide with excellent outcomes. Standard AML induction is cytarabine with an anthracycline; FLT3 and IDH inhibitors target specific mutations. Favourable cytogenetics include t(8;21) and inv(16); monosomy 7 and complex karyotypes are adverse.

**Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)** peaks at 2-5 years and is the commonest childhood cancer. Features include lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, mediastinal mass (T-cell ALL) and CNS involvement. Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) confers a poor prognosis but responds to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Treatment involves induction, consolidation, CNS-directed intrathecal methotrexate and prolonged maintenance; blinatumomab and CAR-T therapy are used in relapse.

## Chronic leukaemias

**Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)** is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase in over 95 percent. Peak age 40-60. Massive splenomegaly, a very high white cell count with the full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, basophilia and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score. Imatinib and second-generation inhibitors (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib) have transformed survival; response is monitored by quantitative BCR-ABL PCR. Blast crisis is transformation to acute leukaemia.

**Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)** is the commonest leukaemia in the Western world, a clonal proliferation of mature B cells (CD5, CD19, CD23 positive). Often an incidental lymphocytosis in an older patient; smear (smudge) cells on the film. Complications: warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent infection, and Richter transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Binet or Rai staging guides treatment; asymptomatic early-stage disease is observed. Treatment options include BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib), venetoclax with obinutuzumab, and chemoimmunotherapy. Deletion 17p or TP53 mutation predicts poor response to chemotherapy.

## Hodgkin lymphoma

Bimodal age distribution (20s and over 60). Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15 and CD30 positive, binucleate owl's eye appearance) in a background of reactive cells. Painless cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, alcohol-induced nodal pain, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, over 10 percent weight loss) and Pel-Ebstein fever. Nodular sclerosing is the commonest subtype; lymphocyte-rich has the best prognosis and lymphocyte-depleted the worst. Associated with EBV. Staged by Ann Arbor classification with PET-CT. Treatment is ABVD chemotherapy (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) with or without radiotherapy, with cure rates above 80 percent; brentuximab vedotin (anti-CD30) and checkpoint inhibitors for relapse. Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis and doxorubicin cardiomyopathy.

## Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

| Subtype | Key features |
|---|---|
| Diffuse large B-cell | Commonest; aggressive; R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone) |
| Follicular | Indolent; t(14;18) BCL2 overexpression; watch and wait or rituximab-based therapy |
| Mantle cell | t(11;14) cyclin D1; older men; aggressive |
| Burkitt | t(8;14) MYC; starry sky appearance; EBV-associated endemic form; very high tumour lysis risk |
| Marginal zone (MALT) | Gastric MALT linked to Helicobacter pylori; eradication may cure |
| Adult T-cell | HTLV-1; Japan and Caribbean |
| Mycosis fungoides | Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma |

Risk factors for NHL include HIV, EBV, immunosuppression after transplantation, Helicobacter pylori, hepatitis C, Sjogren syndrome, coeliac disease (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma) and Hashimoto thyroiditis.

## Key points

- Auer rods indicate AML; t(15;17) promyelocytic leukaemia presents with DIC and responds to ATRA
- Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) defines CML and marks poor-risk ALL; tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the treatment
- CLL: smudge cells, CD5 and CD23 positive B cells, warm haemolysis and Richter transformation
- Reed-Sternberg cells and alcohol-induced nodal pain point to Hodgkin lymphoma treated with ABVD
- t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell, t(8;14) Burkitt
- Gastric MALT lymphoma may regress with Helicobacter pylori eradication

title: HIV infection
summary: Natural history, testing, antiretroviral therapy, opportunistic infections by CD4 count and prevention strategies including PEP and PrEP.
content:
## Overview

HIV is an RNA retrovirus that infects CD4-positive T lymphocytes via the CD4 receptor and CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptors, using reverse transcriptase to produce proviral DNA that integrates into the host genome. Around 110,000 people live with HIV in the UK; effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) now confers near-normal life expectancy and renders the virus untransmissible when the viral load is undetectable.

## Natural history

- Seroconversion illness 2-6 weeks after exposure in 60-80 percent: fever, pharyngitis, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers, lymphopenia, occasionally aseptic meningitis. Very high viral load and high infectivity
- Asymptomatic phase lasting years with gradual CD4 decline of about 50-80 cells per year
- Symptomatic disease and AIDS when CD4 falls below 200 cells/mm3 or an AIDS-defining illness occurs

## Testing

Fourth-generation combined antigen-antibody assays detect p24 antigen and antibody with a window period of about 45 days (a negative test at 4 weeks is reassuring; repeat at 12 weeks after high-risk exposure if the first was within the window). Reactive screens are confirmed by a second assay; HIV RNA PCR is used for early infection and infant diagnosis. UK guidance recommends opt-out testing in emergency departments in high-prevalence areas and testing for indicator conditions (tuberculosis, lymphoma, unexplained cytopenia, seborrhoeic dermatitis, shingles in the young, oral candidiasis).

## Antiretroviral therapy

Everyone with HIV should start ART regardless of CD4 count, ideally within two weeks of diagnosis. Standard regimens combine two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors with a third agent, most often an integrase inhibitor.

| Class | Examples | Notable adverse effects |
|---|---|---|
| NRTI | Tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, zidovudine | Tenofovir disoproxil: renal tubular damage, osteopenia; abacavir: hypersensitivity if HLA-B*57:01; zidovudine: anaemia, lipoatrophy |
| NNRTI | Efavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine | Efavirenz: neuropsychiatric effects, rash |
| Integrase inhibitors | Dolutegravir, bictegravir, raltegravir, cabotegravir | Weight gain, insomnia; dolutegravir raises creatinine slightly |
| Protease inhibitors | Darunavir, atazanavir (boosted by ritonavir or cobicistat) | Dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance, CYP3A4 inhibition; atazanavir: unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia |
| Entry inhibitors | Maraviroc (CCR5), enfuvirtide | |

Long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine every two months is an option for stable suppressed patients. Monitor viral load (undetectable within 3-6 months) and CD4. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome may cause paradoxical worsening of opportunistic infection in the weeks after starting ART.

## Opportunistic infections by CD4 count

- Below 200: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (dry cough, exertional desaturation, bilateral interstitial infiltrates; co-trimoxazole treatment and prophylaxis, steroids if PaO2 below 9.3 kPa), oesophageal candidiasis, tuberculosis at any count
- Below 100: cerebral toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions; pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine), cryptococcal meningitis (India ink, cryptococcal antigen; liposomal amphotericin and flucytosine, then fluconazole), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus), cryptosporidium diarrhoea
- Below 50: cytomegalovirus retinitis (pizza-pie fundus; ganciclovir or valganciclovir), disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (azithromycin prophylaxis), primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-driven, single lesion)
- Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma can occur at any count

Start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 falls below 200.

## Prevention

Post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir-emtricitabine plus raltegravir or dolutegravir for 28 days, started within 72 hours. Pre-exposure prophylaxis with daily or event-based tenofovir-emtricitabine is highly effective and available on the NHS. Vertical transmission falls below 0.5 percent with maternal ART, an undetectable viral load allowing vaginal delivery, neonatal zidovudine and avoidance of breastfeeding (though supported breastfeeding is now possible in the UK with undetectable viral load).

## Key points

- Fourth-generation tests detect antigen and antibody with a 45-day window period
- Start ART in everyone at diagnosis: two NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor is standard
- Test HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir; tenofovir disoproxil affects kidneys and bone
- Pneumocystis appears below CD4 200, toxoplasma and cryptococcus below 100, CMV and MAC below 50
- Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 falls below 200
- PEP within 72 hours for 28 days; undetectable viral load means untransmissible

title: Tuberculosis
summary: Pathogenesis, clinical spectrum, diagnosis of active and latent infection, standard and extended treatment regimens and the adverse effects of first-line antituberculous drugs.
content:
## Overview

Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an aerobic, slow-growing, acid-fast bacillus transmitted by inhalation of droplet nuclei. Around a quarter of the world population is latently infected; the UK sees around 4,500 cases a year, concentrated in people born abroad, the homeless, prisoners, and those with HIV or immunosuppression. The lifetime risk of reactivation is 5-10 percent, rising to 10 percent per year with untreated HIV.

## Pathogenesis

Alveolar macrophages ingest the bacilli, which resist killing and provoke a T-helper-1 response with granuloma formation and caseating necrosis. Primary infection is usually contained (Ghon focus and hilar nodes forming the Ghon complex) but may progress in the immunocompromised.
