Post-primary disease arises from reactivation, classically in the well-oxygenated upper lobes.

## Clinical features

Pulmonary TB: cough for more than three weeks, haemoptysis, night sweats, fever, weight loss, upper zone consolidation or cavitation on chest X-ray. Extrapulmonary sites include lymph nodes (commonest extrapulmonary site, painless cervical lymphadenopathy with cold abscess), pleura (lymphocytic exudate with raised adenosine deaminase), bone and spine (Pott disease), genitourinary tract (sterile pyuria), CNS (tuberculous meningitis with basal enhancement, cranial nerve palsies, low CSF glucose and high protein), pericardium, gastrointestinal tract and adrenals. Miliary TB describes haematogenous dissemination with millet-seed shadowing.

## Diagnosis

- Three sputum samples (one early morning) for microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine) and culture; culture on liquid media takes 2-6 weeks and provides drug susceptibility
- Nucleic acid amplification (GeneXpert) detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within hours
- Bronchoscopy or induced sputum if no spontaneous sputum; biopsy of extrapulmonary sites shows caseating granulomas
- Histology, CSF or pleural fluid testing as appropriate; test for HIV in all cases

## Latent tuberculosis

Defined by immune sensitisation without active disease. Screen contacts, new entrants from high-incidence countries, healthcare workers and patients before anti-TNF therapy using an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or Mantoux test. IGRA is unaffected by BCG. Treat with 3 months of isoniazid and rifampicin or 6 months of isoniazid, after excluding active disease with a chest X-ray.

## Treatment of active tuberculosis

Standard regimen: 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid (2RHZE/4RH). CNS TB requires 12 months in total with adjunctive dexamethasone; pericardial disease also receives steroids. Pyridoxine is co-prescribed to prevent isoniazid neuropathy. Directly observed therapy is used for those at risk of non-adherence.

| Drug | Key adverse effects |
|---|---|
| Rifampicin | Hepatitis, orange secretions, potent CYP450 induction (contraceptive and warfarin failure), flu-like syndrome |
| Isoniazid | Peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis, agranulocytosis, drug-induced lupus, CYP inhibition |
| Pyrazinamide | Hyperuricaemia and gout, hepatitis, arthralgia |
| Ethambutol | Optic neuritis with loss of colour vision and visual acuity; check acuity first and adjust dose in renal impairment |

Check liver function at baseline and monitor; if transaminases exceed five times normal or the patient is symptomatic, stop and reintroduce drugs sequentially. Patients with smear-positive pulmonary disease are considered non-infectious after two weeks of treatment. Notify all cases to the UK Health Security Agency and trace contacts.

## Drug resistance

Multidrug-resistant TB is resistant to at least rifampicin and isoniazid; extensively drug-resistant TB adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone and a second-line injectable or bedaquiline or linezolid. Shorter all-oral regimens based on bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) are now standard for MDR-TB in specialist care.

## Key points

- Upper lobe cavitation, cough over three weeks and night sweats in a high-risk patient should prompt three sputum samples
- IGRA identifies latent infection and is unaffected by BCG; treat latent TB with 3 months of rifampicin and isoniazid
- Standard therapy is 2 months of RHZE then 4 months of RH; extend to 12 months with steroids for CNS disease
- Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, pyrazinamide gout, isoniazid neuropathy and rifampicin enzyme induction
- Always test for HIV and notify the case
- Rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert flags probable MDR-TB

title: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack
summary: Vascular territory syndromes, hyperacute management including thrombolysis and thrombectomy criteria, TIA assessment and secondary prevention according to UK guidance.
content:
## Overview

Stroke is the fourth leading cause of death in the UK and the largest single cause of complex adult disability. Around 85 percent of strokes are ischaemic (thrombotic, embolic or lacunar) and 15 percent haemorrhagic (intracerebral or subarachnoid). A transient ischaemic attack is a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal ischaemia without infarction; the time-based 24-hour definition has been replaced by a tissue-based one.

## Clinical syndromes

The Oxford (Bamford) classification divides ischaemic stroke by the territory affected.

| Syndrome | Features |
|---|---|
| Total anterior circulation (TACS) | All three of: contralateral hemiparesis or sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect) |
| Partial anterior circulation (PACS) | Two of the three above |
| Lacunar (LACS) | Pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis; no cortical signs |
| Posterior circulation (POCS) | Cerebellar or brainstem signs, isolated hemianopia, cranial nerve palsy with contralateral motor or sensory deficit |

Specific patterns: anterior cerebral artery involvement affects the contralateral leg more than the arm; middle cerebral artery affects face and arm with dysphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant); posterior cerebral artery produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome causes ipsilateral Horner, facial sensory loss and ataxia with contralateral body sensory loss. Weber syndrome pairs an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis. Locked-in syndrome follows basilar occlusion.

## Hyperacute management of ischaemic stroke

- Immediate non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage; CT angiography if thrombectomy is being considered
- Alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset if haemorrhage is excluded and there are no contraindications (recent surgery or bleeding, anticoagulation with INR above 1.7, blood pressure above 185/110, previous intracranial haemorrhage)
- Mechanical thrombectomy for proximal anterior circulation occlusion within 6 hours (together with thrombolysis if eligible), extended to 24 hours when perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue; also considered for basilar occlusion
- Aspirin 300 mg daily for two weeks once haemorrhage is excluded (24 hours after thrombolysis), then long-term antiplatelet
- Swallow screen before oral intake, maintain glucose 4-11 mmol/L, treat fever, do not lower blood pressure acutely unless thrombolysis is planned or there is hypertensive emergency
- Decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours for malignant middle cerebral artery infarction in appropriate patients

## Haemorrhagic stroke

Reverse anticoagulation immediately (prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors). Lower systolic blood pressure rapidly to 130-140 mmHg within an hour if presenting within six hours. Neurosurgical referral for cerebellar haematoma, hydrocephalus or deteriorating consciousness.

## Transient ischaemic attack

Give aspirin 300 mg immediately and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours for all suspected TIA regardless of ABCD2 score, which is no longer used to triage. Imaging is MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences; carotid imaging within 24 hours. Carotid endarterectomy within two weeks for symptomatic stenosis of 50-99 percent (NASCET criteria). Do not drive for one month after TIA or stroke.

## Secondary prevention

Clopidogrel 75 mg daily is first-line antiplatelet after ischaemic stroke or TIA (aspirin plus dipyridamole if clopidogrel is not tolerated). Short-course dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days is recommended for minor stroke or high-risk TIA. High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg. Blood pressure target below 130/80. Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation, starting immediately after TIA and around 14 days after disabling stroke. Manage diabetes, smoking and lifestyle. Consider closure of a patent foramen ovale in patients under 60 with an otherwise unexplained stroke.

## Key points

- Bamford classification: TACS requires hemiparesis, hemianopia and cortical dysfunction together
- Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy within 6 hours routinely and up to 24 hours with favourable imaging
- Aspirin 300 mg for two weeks, then clopidogrel 75 mg long term
- All suspected TIA needs aspirin immediately and specialist review within 24 hours
- Carotid endarterectomy within two weeks for symptomatic 50-99 percent stenosis
- Reverse anticoagulation and lower blood pressure promptly in intracerebral haemorrhage

title: Epilepsy and seizures
summary: Seizure classification, differential diagnosis, first-line antiseizure medication by seizure type, status epilepticus management and driving regulations.
content:
## Overview

Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or after one seizure with a high (over 60 percent) recurrence risk. Prevalence in the UK is about 1 percent. Part 1 questions test classification, drug selection, adverse effects, status epilepticus and driving law, with a strong emphasis on women of childbearing potential.

## Classification (ILAE 2017)

- Focal onset: aware or impaired awareness; motor or non-motor; may progress to bilateral tonic-clonic. Temporal lobe seizures produce epigastric rising, deja vu, olfactory hallucinations and automatisms; frontal lobe seizures produce Jacksonian march and Todd paresis
- Generalised onset: tonic-clonic, absence (3 Hz spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation), myoclonic, atonic, tonic
- Unknown onset

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy presents in adolescence with early morning myoclonic jerks, generalised seizures after sleep deprivation and alcohol; it responds to sodium valproate or levetiracetam and requires lifelong treatment.

## Differential diagnosis

Syncope (brief, pallor, rapid recovery, may have a few myoclonic jerks), cardiac arrhythmia, functional (dissociative) seizures (long duration, eyes closed, asynchronous movements, pelvic thrusting, no post-ictal confusion, normal lactate and prolactin), hypoglycaemia, transient ischaemic attack, migraine, parasomnias. Tongue biting (lateral), incontinence, post-ictal confusion and a raised prolactin or lactate favour epileptic seizure.

## Investigations

ECG in every first seizure to exclude long QT and other arrhythmias. EEG supports classification but a normal interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. MRI brain is the imaging of choice, urgently if focal onset, age over 25 at first seizure, or focal neurology.

## Antiseizure medication

Treatment usually starts after a second seizure, or after a first seizure with structural abnormality, abnormal EEG or high recurrence risk.

| Seizure type | First line | Second line or alternatives |
|---|---|---|
| Generalised tonic-clonic | Sodium valproate (men, or women not of childbearing potential); lamotrigine or levetiracetam otherwise | Clobazam, perampanel, topiramate |
| Focal | Lamotrigine or levetiracetam | Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide |
| Absence | Ethosuximide | Sodium valproate, lamotrigine, levetiracetam |
| Myoclonic | Sodium valproate (as above) | Levetiracetam |
| Tonic or atonic | Sodium valproate (as above) | Lamotrigine |

Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and pregabalin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.

Adverse effects to know: sodium valproate (teratogenic with neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm, weight gain, hair loss, tremor, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonaemia; the MHRA prohibits initiation in anyone under 55 unless two specialists agree no alternative exists), lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially with rapid titration or concurrent valproate), carbamazepine (hyponatraemia, agranulocytosis, enzyme induction, HLA-B*15:02 and SJS in Han Chinese), phenytoin (gingival hypertrophy, hirsutism, cerebellar ataxia, zero-order kinetics), levetiracetam (irritability and mood change), topiramate (weight loss, renal stones, acute glaucoma, cognitive slowing), vigabatrin (visual field defects).

## Status epilepticus

Defined operationally as a seizure lasting over 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery. Protect the airway, give oxygen, check glucose. First line: intravenous lorazepam 4 mg (repeated once after 5-10 minutes) or buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community. Second line at 20-30 minutes: levetiracetam, sodium valproate or phenytoin infusion (fosphenytoin). Third line: general anaesthesia with propofol or thiopental and intensive care. Give thiamine if alcohol misuse is suspected and consider pyridoxine, eclampsia and non-convulsive status.

## Driving (Group 1 licence)

First unprovoked seizure: no driving for 6 months (12 months if abnormal EEG or imaging). Established epilepsy: seizure-free for 12 months. Seizures only during sleep for at least 12 months (or 3 years if previously awake seizures) may permit driving. Withdrawal of medication: no driving during withdrawal and for 6 months afterwards. Group 2 licences require 10 years seizure-free and off medication.

## Key points

- Diagnosis is clinical; ECG in every first seizure, MRI for focal or late-onset epilepsy
- Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first line for focal seizures and for generalised seizures in women of childbearing potential
- Sodium valproate is the most effective drug for generalised epilepsy but is restricted because of teratogenicity
- Carbamazepine worsens absence and myoclonic seizures; ethosuximide is first line for absence
- Status epilepticus: lorazepam, then levetiracetam, valproate or phenytoin, then anaesthesia
- Stop driving for 6 months after a first seizure and 12 months after any seizure in established epilepsy

title: Oncological emergencies
summary: Recognition and initial management of neutropenic sepsis, malignant spinal cord compression, hypercalcaemia, superior vena cava obstruction, tumour lysis syndrome and raised intracranial pressure.
content:
## Overview

Oncological emergencies arise from the tumour itself, from its metabolic consequences or from treatment. They are favourite exam material because the correct first step is time-critical and evidence-based. Most present to acute general medicine rather than to oncology, so every physician must recognise them.

## Neutropenic sepsis

Defined by neutrophils of 0.5 x 10^9/L or below and a temperature above 38 degrees or other signs of sepsis, typically 7-14 days after chemotherapy. Give empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam within one hour, before results are available; add an aminoglycoside if unstable and consider a glycopeptide for line infection or MRSA colonisation. Do not delay for a neutrophil count if the patient is unwell. The MASCC score identifies low-risk patients who may be managed with oral antibiotics. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor prophylaxis is used with high-risk regimens; fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is offered during expected neutropenia in acute leukaemia and stem cell transplantation.

## Malignant spinal cord compression

Occurs in 5 percent of cancer patients, most often from vertebral metastases of prostate, breast, lung, renal cancer, myeloma and lymphoma. Back pain (often thoracic, worse on coughing or lying flat) precedes weakness, sensory level and sphincter disturbance. Any cancer patient with new back pain and neurological symptoms needs whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, dexamethasone 16 mg daily with gastroprotection immediately, and discussion with oncology and spinal surgery for radiotherapy or decompression within 24 hours. Neurological status at presentation is the strongest predictor of outcome. Cauda equina compression produces lower motor neuron signs and saddle anaesthesia.

## Hypercalcaemia of malignancy

Caused by PTH-related peptide (squamous cell lung cancer, renal, breast), osteolytic metastases and myeloma, or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D from lymphoma. Symptoms: thirst, polyuria, constipation, confusion, nausea, bone pain, shortened QT. Treat with 3-4 litres of intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 24 hours, then intravenous zoledronic acid, which takes 2-4 days for maximal effect. Denosumab for bisphosphonate-refractory cases; calcitonin for rapid short-term reduction; steroids for lymphoma and myeloma. Stop thiazides and calcium or vitamin D supplements.

## Superior vena cava obstruction

Lung cancer (especially small cell), lymphoma and thymoma cause facial and arm swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins, headache worse on stooping, and a positive Pemberton sign. CT venography confirms. Sit the patient up, give dexamethasone and arrange endovascular stenting for rapid relief; radiotherapy or chemotherapy follows depending on histology. Obtain tissue before steroids if lymphoma is possible and the patient is stable.

## Tumour lysis syndrome

Rapid cell breakdown after chemotherapy for bulky, chemosensitive tumours such as Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukaemia and high-grade lymphoma releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids. Cairo-Bishop laboratory criteria: uric acid, potassium and phosphate rising 25 percent or above defined thresholds, with hypocalcaemia; clinical criteria add creatinine rise, arrhythmia or seizure. Prevent with hyperhydration and allopurinol for intermediate risk or rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase, contraindicated in G6PD deficiency) for high risk. Treat hyperkalaemia conventionally and dialyse for refractory abnormalities.

## Raised intracranial pressure from brain metastases

Headache worse in the morning and on lying, vomiting, focal deficit, seizures or reduced consciousness. Give dexamethasone 8-16 mg daily and obtain CT or MRI. Whole-brain or stereotactic radiotherapy, surgery for solitary lesions, and levetiracetam for seizures (not primary prophylaxis).

## Immune-related adverse events

Checkpoint inhibitors cause colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and myocarditis. Grade 2 or higher toxicity is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and withholding the drug; infliximab for steroid-refractory colitis.

| Emergency | First critical action |
|---|---|
| Neutropenic sepsis | Piperacillin-tazobactam within one hour |
| Spinal cord compression | Dexamethasone 16 mg and MRI whole spine within 24 hours |
| Hypercalcaemia | Intravenous saline then zoledronic acid |
| SVC obstruction | Dexamethasone, sit up, stenting |
| Tumour lysis | Fluids, rasburicase or allopurinol, monitor electrolytes |

## Key points

- Neutropenic sepsis is treated empirically within the hour; do not wait for the blood count
- New back pain with neurological symptoms in a cancer patient means dexamethasone now and MRI within 24 hours
- Hypercalcaemia: rehydrate first, bisphosphonate second
- Endovascular stenting gives the fastest relief of SVC obstruction
- Rasburicase prevents tumour lysis in high-risk patients but is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
- Immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity is treated with high-dose steroids

title: Tumour markers and paraneoplastic syndromes
summary: The clinical uses and limitations of serum tumour markers, and the endocrine, neurological, dermatological and haematological paraneoplastic syndromes associated with common cancers.
content:
## Overview

Tumour markers are substances produced by tumours or by the body in response to them. Most lack the sensitivity and specificity for population screening but are valuable for prognosis, monitoring response and detecting relapse. Paraneoplastic syndromes are remote effects of cancer not caused by local invasion or metastasis, mediated by hormones, cytokines or cross-reactive antibodies; they may be the presenting feature and can precede the tumour by years.

## Serum tumour markers

| Marker | Principal cancers | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) | Hepatocellular carcinoma, non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (yolk sac elements) | Also raised in pregnancy, cirrhosis, hepatitis; used with ultrasound in HCC surveillance |
| Beta-hCG | Gestational trophoblastic disease, choriocarcinoma, germ cell tumours (both seminoma and non-seminoma) | Pure seminoma never raises AFP |
| CA-125 | Ovarian cancer | Raised by endometriosis, ascites, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation, peritoneal TB; part of the NICE ovarian pathway with ultrasound and the Risk of Malignancy Index |
| CA 19-9 | Pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma | Raised in cholestasis; absent in Lewis antigen-negative individuals |
| CEA | Colorectal cancer | Smoking, IBD and cirrhosis raise levels; useful for post-resection surveillance, not diagnosis |
| PSA | Prostate cancer | Raised by benign hyperplasia, prostatitis, urinary retention, ejaculation, cycling and instrumentation; free-to-total ratio and MRI refine risk |
| Calcitonin | Medullary thyroid carcinoma | Screening in MEN2 kindreds |
| Thyroglobulin | Differentiated thyroid cancer follow-up after thyroidectomy | |
| Chromogranin A, urinary 5-HIAA | Neuroendocrine tumours, carcinoid | |
| LDH | Lymphoma, germ cell tumours, melanoma | Prognostic rather than diagnostic |
| Beta-2 microglobulin | Myeloma, lymphoma | Prognostic |
| S100, LDH | Melanoma | |
| CA 15-3 | Breast cancer monitoring | |
| Paraprotein, serum free light chains | Myeloma | |

Alkaline phosphatase (bony) and hypercalcaemia point towards skeletal metastases in any cancer.

## Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes

- SIADH: small cell lung cancer is the classic cause, producing euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine; treat with fluid restriction, demeclocycline or tolvaptan
- Ectopic ACTH: small cell lung cancer and bronchial carcinoid; hypokalaemic alkalosis, pigmentation and rapid onset dominate over classical cushingoid habitus
- Hypercalcaemia via PTH-related peptide: squamous cell lung cancer, renal cell, breast, head and neck squamous cancers
- Hypoglycaemia from insulin-like growth factor 2: large mesenchymal tumours and hepatocellular carcinoma
- Polycythaemia from erythropoietin: renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, uterine fibroids
- Gynaecomastia and hyperthyroidism from beta-hCG: germ cell tumours
- Carcinoid syndrome: flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm and right heart valve fibrosis, usually only after hepatic metastasis bypasses first-pass metabolism

## Neurological paraneoplastic syndromes

- Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, small cell lung cancer, proximal weakness that improves with exercise, hyporeflexia, autonomic features; treat with 3,4-diaminopyridine
- Subacute cerebellar degeneration: anti-Yo (breast, ovary), anti-Hu (small cell lung cancer)
- Limbic encephalitis: anti-Hu and anti-Ma2 with lung and testicular tumours; anti-NMDA receptor with ovarian teratoma
- Sensory neuronopathy (anti-Hu), opsoclonus-myoclonus (neuroblastoma in children, breast in adults), dermatomyositis (see below), peripheral neuropathy with myeloma and POEMS syndrome

## Dermatological and haematological syndromes

Acanthosis nigricans (gastric adenocarcinoma), dermatomyositis (ovarian, lung, gastric and pancreatic cancer in about 20 percent of adults), acquired ichthyosis (lymphoma), erythema gyratum repens (lung), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), sweet syndrome (AML), migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of pancreatic cancer), sign of Leser-Trelat (sudden eruptive seborrhoeic keratoses), pruritus (Hodgkin lymphoma, polycythaemia). Haematological manifestations include venous thromboembolism, disseminated intravascular coagulation (acute promyelocytic leukaemia, adenocarcinoma), microangiopathic haemolysis, eosinophilia and thrombocytosis.

## Key points

- Tumour markers are for monitoring and prognosis, not for screening asymptomatic patients
- AFP is never raised by pure seminoma; beta-hCG may be raised by either germ cell type
- Small cell lung cancer causes SIADH, ectopic ACTH and Lambert-Eaton; squamous lung cancer causes PTHrP hypercalcaemia
- Anti-Yo suggests breast or ovarian cancer; anti-Hu suggests small cell lung cancer
- Adults with dermatomyositis need a cancer screen
- Renal cell carcinoma produces erythropoietin and polycythaemia

title: The acute red eye
summary: A systematic approach to conjunctivitis, keratitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis and acute angle-closure glaucoma, including the systemic associations physicians must recognise.
content:
## Overview

The red eye ranges from trivial conjunctivitis to sight-threatening glaucoma, keratitis and uveitis. Physicians must distinguish conditions safely managed in primary care from those requiring same-day ophthalmology review, and recognise when a red eye is the presenting feature of a systemic inflammatory disease.

## Triage: features suggesting serious disease

- Reduced visual acuity
- Moderate to severe pain or photophobia
- Ciliary (circumcorneal) injection rather than diffuse conjunctival redness
- Corneal opacity or fluorescein staining
- Fixed or irregular pupil
- Hypopyon
- Contact lens wear

## Differential diagnosis

| Condition | Pain | Vision | Discharge | Pupil | Key signs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bacterial conjunctivitis | Gritty | Normal | Purulent | Normal | Diffuse redness, lids stuck in morning |
| Viral conjunctivitis | Gritty | Normal | Watery | Normal | Preauricular node, follicles, often bilateral, adenovirus |
| Allergic conjunctivitis | Itch | Normal | Watery, stringy | Normal | Chemosis, papillae, atopy |
| Keratitis | Severe | Reduced | Watery or purulent | Normal | Corneal ulcer staining with fluorescein; dendritic in herpes simplex |
| Anterior uveitis | Aching, photophobia | Reduced | None | Small, irregular, poorly reactive | Ciliary flush, cells and flare, hypopyon, synechiae |
| Episcleritis | Mild ache | Normal | None | Normal | Sectoral redness that blanches with phenylephrine, mobile vessels |
| Scleritis | Severe, boring, wakes at night | May be reduced | None | Normal | Deep bluish redness, tender globe, does not blanch |
| Acute angle-closure glaucoma | Severe with headache, nausea | Markedly reduced, haloes | None | Mid-dilated, fixed | Hazy cornea, hard globe, raised pressure |
| Subconjunctival haemorrhage | None | Normal | None | Normal | Bright red patch; check blood pressure and anticoagulation |

## Conjunctivitis

Bacterial conjunctivitis is usually self-limiting; chloramphenicol drops shorten the course. Adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious. Chlamydial conjunctivitis causes chronic follicular disease in young adults and needs systemic azithromycin or doxycycline with sexual health referral. Gonococcal conjunctivitis is hyperacute with copious pus and threatens the cornea.

## Keratitis

Bacterial keratitis is strongly associated with contact lens wear (Pseudomonas) and needs urgent scraping and intensive topical antibiotics. Herpes simplex keratitis shows a dendritic ulcer on fluorescein; treat with topical aciclovir and avoid topical steroids, which cause geographic ulceration. Acanthamoeba keratitis affects lens wearers exposed to water and causes pain out of proportion to signs. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson sign on the nose tip) needs oral antivirals within 72 hours.

## Anterior uveitis

Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body. Half of cases are HLA-B27 associated: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. Other causes include sarcoidosis (often bilateral and granulomatous), Behcet disease (hypopyon), juvenile idiopathic arthritis, herpes viruses, syphilis, tuberculosis and TINU syndrome. Treat with topical steroids and a cycloplegic (cyclopentolate) to relieve pain and prevent posterior synechiae. Recurrent or bilateral uveitis warrants a systemic work-up including chest X-ray, HLA-B27, ACE, syphilis serology and inflammatory markers.

## Scleritis and episcleritis

Episcleritis is benign, self-limiting and treated with lubricants or oral NSAIDs. Scleritis is a vasculitic process that threatens sight; half of patients have systemic disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, relapsing polychondritis, SLE and inflammatory bowel disease. Necrotising scleritis with rheumatoid arthritis carries a poor prognosis. Treat with oral NSAIDs, systemic steroids and immunosuppression; refer urgently.

## Acute angle-closure glaucoma

Typically an older, long-sighted patient, often in dim light or after mydriatic or anticholinergic drugs. Treat immediately with intravenous acetazolamide, topical pilocarpine to constrict the pupil, topical beta-blocker and steroid, lying flat, and analgesia and antiemetics. Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy to both eyes.

## Key points

- Reduced acuity, photophobia, ciliary flush or an abnormal pupil signal serious disease requiring same-day ophthalmology review
- Contact lens wearers with a painful red eye have bacterial keratitis until proven otherwise
- Never give topical steroids to an undiagnosed red eye because of herpes simplex risk
- Anterior uveitis is HLA-B27 associated; treat with topical steroids and cycloplegics
- Scleritis is painful, deep, non-blanching and linked to rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis
- Acute angle-closure glaucoma is treated with acetazolamide, pilocarpine and laser iridotomy

title: Diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy
summary: Classification, screening and treatment of diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy, and the grading and significance of hypertensive retinal changes.
content:
## Overview

Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of preventable sight loss in working-age adults in the UK. Hypertensive retinopathy provides a window on systemic end-organ damage and can indicate a hypertensive emergency. Both are examined through fundal descriptions and questions on management thresholds.

## Diabetic retinopathy: pathophysiology

Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillary pericytes and endothelium, causing microaneurysm formation, increased permeability (haemorrhage, exudate, oedema) and capillary occlusion with retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina secretes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), driving new vessel formation (neovascularisation) which bleeds and fibroses, leading to vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. Risk factors: duration of diabetes, poor glycaemic control, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, nephropathy, pregnancy, smoking and rapid intensification of glycaemic control (transient worsening).

## Classification

| Grade | Features |
|---|---|
| R0 None | Normal fundus |
| R1 Background (mild non-proliferative) | Microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates |
| R2 Pre-proliferative (moderate to severe non-proliferative) | Cotton wool spots, venous beading and loops, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA), multiple deep haemorrhages |
| R3 Proliferative | New vessels on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage, fibrous tissue, tractional detachment |
| M1 Maculopathy | Exudates or thickening within one disc diameter of the fovea; clinically significant macular oedema |

Proliferative disease is more common in type 1 diabetes; maculopathy is the commoner cause of visual loss in type 2. Rubeosis iridis (iris neovascularisation) leads to neovascular glaucoma.

## Screening

The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme invites everyone with diabetes aged 12 and over for digital retinal photography, annually or every two years for those with two consecutive normal screens. Pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes are screened at booking and again at 28 weeks. Grade R2, R3 or M1 triggers referral to hospital eye services; R3 with new vessels or haemorrhage is urgent.

## Treatment

- Optimise glycaemic control (HbA1c target individualised, typically 48-58 mmol/mol), blood pressure (below 140/80, or 130/80 with complications) and lipids; fenofibrate slows progression
- Proliferative retinopathy: pan-retinal photocoagulation reduces VEGF drive by ablating ischaemic peripheral retina; side effects include reduced peripheral and night vision. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab) are an alternative or adjunct
- Diabetic macular oedema with central involvement: intravitreal anti-VEGF injections first line; intravitreal dexamethasone or fluocinolone implants for poor responders or pseudophakic eyes; focal laser for non-central oedema
- Vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional detachment
- Sudden visual loss in a diabetic patient may also be due to vitreous haemorrhage, retinal vein occlusion or ischaemic optic neuropathy

## Hypertensive retinopathy

Keith-Wagener-Barker grading:

- Grade 1: generalised arteriolar narrowing, silver or copper wiring
- Grade 2: focal arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping
- Grade 3: flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates (a macular star)
- Grade 4: grade 3 plus papilloedema (swollen optic disc)

Grades 3 and 4 indicate accelerated (malignant) hypertension, defined by severe hypertension (usually above 180/120 mmHg) with retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema, and demand same-day assessment with careful blood pressure reduction to avoid watershed cerebral infarction. Hypertension also predisposes to retinal vein occlusion, retinal artery occlusion and anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

## Other vascular retinopathies

Central retinal vein occlusion produces a stormy sunset fundus with widespread haemorrhages and disc swelling; check for hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma and hyperviscosity. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision with a cherry red spot and pale retina; it is a stroke equivalent, mandating exclusion of giant cell arteritis and carotid disease.

## Key points

- Microaneurysms and hard exudates are background changes; cotton wool spots, venous beading and IRMA mark pre-proliferative disease; new vessels define proliferative retinopathy
- Maculopathy is the leading cause of visual loss in type 2 diabetes
- Annual screening from age 12 in the NHS programme; refer R2, R3 and M1
- Pan-retinal photocoagulation for proliferative disease; anti-VEGF for central macular oedema
- Arteriovenous nipping is grade 2 and papilloedema grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy
- Retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema with severe hypertension define accelerated hypertension

specialty: Palliative Medicine & End of Life Care
title: Pain management and opioid prescribing in palliative care
summary: The WHO analgesic ladder, starting and titrating strong opioids, breakthrough dosing, opioid conversion ratios, adjuvant analgesics and prescribing in renal impairment.
content:
## Overview

Pain affects up to 70 percent of patients with advanced cancer and is often undertreated. Effective management rests on a careful assessment of each pain (site, character, mechanism), a structured approach to escalation, and confident use of opioid conversions. Part 1 questions are largely numerical: dose calculation, conversion between routes and drugs, and choosing the safest opioid in organ impairment.

## Assessment

Distinguish nociceptive (somatic or visceral), neuropathic (burning, shooting, allodynia) and incident pain (predictable, movement-related). Consider total pain: physical, psychological, social and spiritual components.

## The WHO analgesic ladder

- Step 1: paracetamol and/or NSAID
- Step 2: weak opioid (codeine 30-60 mg four-hourly, maximum 240 mg daily; dihydrocodeine; tramadol) plus step 1 agents
- Step 3: strong opioid (morphine first line) plus step 1 agents

Adjuvants may be added at any step. In practice, many clinicians move directly from step 1 to low-dose strong opioid because weak opioids offer little advantage over 240 mg codeine, which is approximately equivalent to 24 mg oral morphine.

## Starting strong opioids

NICE recommends oral morphine as the first-line strong opioid. For an opioid-naive patient with normal renal function, start 20-30 mg oral morphine in 24 hours (for example 10-15 mg modified-release twice daily, or 5 mg immediate-release four-hourly) with 5 mg immediate-release for breakthrough pain. Breakthrough dose is one-sixth to one-tenth of the total daily dose. Titrate the regular dose by 30-50 percent every 24 hours according to breakthrough use. Prescribe a regular stimulant laxative (senna with or without a softener) for all patients on opioids, and an antiemetic (haloperidol or metoclopramide) for the first week as needed. Warn about drowsiness, which usually settles within days.

## Opioid conversions

| Conversion | Ratio |
|---|---|
| Oral codeine or dihydrocodeine to oral morphine | Divide by 10 |
| Oral tramadol to oral morphine | Divide by 10 |
| Oral morphine to oral oxycodone | Divide by 1.5 to 2 (BNF uses 2) |
| Oral morphine to subcutaneous morphine | Divide by 2 |
| Oral morphine to subcutaneous diamorphine | Divide by 3 |
| Oral oxycodone to subcutaneous oxycodone | Divide by 2 |
| Oral morphine to transdermal fentanyl | 12 microgram/hour patch is approximately 30 mg oral morphine daily |
| Oral morphine to transdermal buprenorphine | 10 microgram/hour patch is approximately 24 mg oral morphine daily |

When switching between opioids for toxicity, reduce the calculated equivalent dose by 25-50 percent to allow for incomplete cross-tolerance. Fentanyl patches take 12-24 hours to reach effect and persist for a similar period after removal, so continue immediate-release opioid for the first 12 hours and never use patches for unstable pain.

## Opioid toxicity

Drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, hallucinations and respiratory depression. Common precipitants are renal impairment, dehydration, infection and drug interactions. Reduce or omit doses, hydrate, and use naloxone only for respiratory depression, in small titrated doses (for example 40-80 micrograms) to avoid abrupt pain crisis.

## Renal and hepatic impairment

Morphine and codeine accumulate active metabolites in renal failure. For eGFR 30-60, use oxycodone with caution or reduce morphine doses. For eGFR below 30, prefer fentanyl, alfentanil or buprenorphine, which are not renally excreted. Reduce doses and lengthen intervals in hepatic impairment.

## Adjuvant analgesics

- Neuropathic pain: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (dose-adjusted for renal function); dexamethasone for nerve compression
- Bone pain: NSAIDs, single-fraction 8 Gy radiotherapy, bisphosphonates or denosumab
- Liver capsule pain and raised intracranial pressure: dexamethasone
- Muscle spasm: baclofen, diazepam
- Colic: hyoscine butylbromide

## Key points

- Start oral morphine at 20-30 mg per 24 hours with a breakthrough dose of one-sixth of the daily total
- Always co-prescribe a laxative; nausea usually settles and antiemetics can be stopped
- Divide oral morphine by 2 for oral oxycodone or subcutaneous morphine, and by 3 for subcutaneous diamorphine
- A 12 microgram/hour fentanyl patch approximates 30 mg oral morphine daily
- Use fentanyl, alfentanil or buprenorphine when eGFR is below 30
- Reduce the equivalent dose by 25-50 percent when switching opioids because of incomplete cross-tolerance

specialty: Palliative Medicine & End of Life Care
title: Symptom control in the last days of life
summary: Recognising dying, individualised care planning, anticipatory prescribing for pain, breathlessness, agitation, secretions and nausea, syringe drivers and the ethical and legal framework.
content:
## Overview

Care in the final days of life aims to relieve distress, respect the priorities of the dying person and support those close to them. NICE guidance (NG31) and the Leadership Alliance five priorities replaced the Liverpool Care Pathway and stress recognition of dying, communication, shared decision-making, individualised care planning and hydration decisions made with the patient and family.

## Recognising that a person is dying

Signs include profound weakness, reduced consciousness, minimal oral intake, difficulty swallowing medication, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, peripheral mottling, reduced urine output and noisy respiratory secretions. Always consider reversible causes such as opioid toxicity, hypercalcaemia, infection or acute kidney injury, and whether treating them is consistent with the person's wishes. Assess daily; recovery does occur and plans must be revisited.

## Communication and planning

Discuss prognosis honestly, using the patient's preferred language, and ask about preferred place of care and death. Document a Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) or equivalent, including resuscitation status. Check for a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare or an advance decision to refuse treatment. Review all medication and stop anything not contributing to comfort (statins, antihypertensives, anticoagulants in most cases, oral hypoglycaemics). Clinically assisted hydration should be considered on an individual basis; it does not reliably prolong life or relieve thirst, but a trial may be appropriate if the family or patient wish, with review after 12-24 hours.

## Anticipatory prescribing

Prescribe subcutaneous medication in advance for the five common symptoms so that treatment is available without delay, typically as needed initially and then via a continuous subcutaneous infusion (syringe driver) over 24 hours if more than two or three doses are required.

| Symptom | First-line drug (opioid-naive doses) | Alternatives and notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pain | Morphine 2.5-5 mg subcutaneously as required; convert regular oral opioid to a 24-hour infusion (oral morphine divided by 2 for subcutaneous morphine) | Oxycodone if morphine not tolerated; alfentanil or fentanyl in renal failure; remove or continue patches and add breakthrough on top |
| Breathlessness | Morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously as required; midazolam 2.5 mg for associated anxiety | Fan to the face, positioning, oxygen only if hypoxic and it helps symptomatically |
| Nausea and vomiting | Haloperidol 0.5-1.5 mg subcutaneously or levomepromazine 2.5-6.25 mg | Cyclizine for raised intracranial pressure or bowel obstruction; metoclopramide for gastric stasis (avoid in complete obstruction and Parkinson disease); hyoscine butylbromide and octreotide for obstructive vomiting |
| Terminal agitation or restlessness | Midazolam 2.5-5 mg subcutaneously as required (10-60 mg over 24 hours in infusion) | Exclude urinary retention, constipation, pain, hypoxia, nicotine withdrawal; levomepromazine or haloperidol if delirium with psychotic features |
| Respiratory tract secretions | Hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg subcutaneously as required (60-120 mg over 24 hours) or glycopyrronium 200-400 micrograms | Reposition; explain to family that the patient is unlikely to be distressed; hyoscine hydrobromide crosses the blood-brain barrier and may sedate or cause paradoxical agitation |

## Syringe drivers

A continuous subcutaneous infusion delivers a steady drug level when swallowing is unreliable. Common compatible combinations include morphine with midazolam and haloperidol or levomepromazine; check compatibility data and dilute with water for injections (sodium chloride for some drugs). Review the site daily and the prescription every 24 hours, adding the previous day's breakthrough doses to the infusion where appropriate.

## Specific situations

- Massive haemorrhage: dark towels, midazolam 5-10 mg intramuscularly or intravenously, stay with the patient
- Seizures: midazolam subcutaneously or buccally; continue antiepileptics via infusion where possible
- Diabetes: stop oral agents; in type 1, reduce to once-daily long-acting insulin, aiming only to avoid symptomatic hyperglycaemia; deactivate implantable defibrillators

## Key points

- Recognise dying using clinical signs but always exclude reversible causes and review regularly
- Communicate openly and document a ReSPECT plan including resuscitation status
- Prescribe anticipatory subcutaneous medication for pain, breathlessness, nausea, agitation and secretions
- Halve the oral morphine daily dose for a 24-hour subcutaneous morphine infusion
- Midazolam is first line for terminal agitation; hyoscine butylbromide or glycopyrronium for secretions
- Clinically assisted hydration is an individualised decision and should be reviewed at least daily

title: Depression and antidepressant therapy
summary: Diagnostic criteria and severity assessment of depression, NICE stepped care, the pharmacology and adverse effects of antidepressant classes, and management of treatment resistance and special situations.
content:
## Overview

Depression affects around one in six adults. For the MRCP the emphasis falls on diagnosis, the choice and side effects of antidepressants (particularly in patients with medical comorbidity), and the recognition of serious complications such as serotonin syndrome and hyponatraemia.

## Diagnosis

ICD-11 and DSM-5 require at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure, with additional symptoms from: fatigue, poor concentration, low self-esteem, guilt, hopelessness, sleep disturbance (typically early morning waking), appetite and weight change, psychomotor retardation or agitation, reduced libido, and thoughts of death or suicide. Somatic (melancholic) features include anhedonia, diurnal variation with morning worsening, and marked weight loss. Exclude hypothyroidism, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, Cushing syndrome, Addison disease, Parkinson disease, medication effects (beta-blockers, steroids, isotretinoin, interferon) and substance misuse. Psychotic depression carries nihilistic delusions and demands urgent psychiatric involvement.

## Suicide risk

Risk factors: male sex, previous self-harm, psychiatric illness, substance misuse, social isolation, chronic physical illness, recent psychiatric discharge and access to means. Ask directly about ideation and plans.

## NICE stepped care

- Less severe depression (PHQ-9 below 16): guided self-help, group cognitive behavioural therapy, behavioural activation, exercise, mindfulness; antidepressants are not first line unless preferred or there is a history of moderate to severe depression
- More severe depression: combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant, or either alone according to patient preference
- Continue antidepressants for at least 6 months after remission (2 years if recurrent) and withdraw slowly to avoid discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, electric shock sensations, insomnia; worst with paroxetine and venlafaxine)
- Review within 2 weeks of starting (1 week if under 30 or at increased suicide risk)

## Antidepressant classes

| Class | Examples | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| SSRI | Sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine | First line; sertraline preferred after myocardial infarction; citalopram prolongs QT (maximum 40 mg, 20 mg over 65); gastrointestinal upset, sexual dysfunction, hyponatraemia (SIADH) especially in the elderly, bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants; fluoxetine has the longest half-life and is preferred in adolescents |
| SNRI | Venlafaxine, duloxetine | Raise blood pressure; venlafaxine cardiotoxic in overdose; duloxetine also treats neuropathic pain |
| Tricyclics | Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, lofepramine | Anticholinergic effects, postural hypotension, sedation, QT prolongation and lethal in overdose; lofepramine is safest; used in low dose for neuropathic pain |
| Mirtazapine | | Sedation and weight gain useful in insomnia and poor appetite; less sexual dysfunction; rare agranulocytosis |
| MAOI | Phenelzine, moclobemide | Hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich food (cheese, wine); reversible moclobemide safer |

## Serotonin syndrome

Triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating) and altered mental state, developing within hours of a serotonergic drug or interaction (SSRIs with tramadol, linezolid, lithium, triptans, MAOIs, St John's Wort). Stop the drug, cool, give benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine in severe cases. Contrast with neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which develops over days with rigidity, hyporeflexia and raised creatine kinase.

## Treatment-resistant depression

Check adherence and dose, then switch to a different antidepressant, augment with an atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine, aripiprazole), lithium or a second antidepressant (mirtazapine with an SSRI or SNRI), and add psychological therapy. Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective for severe, psychotic or life-threatening depression (refusal to eat or drink) and catatonia; adverse effects are transient retrograde amnesia and headache.

## Special situations

In pregnancy, sertraline is preferred; paroxetine is associated with cardiac malformations and SSRIs late in pregnancy with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. In older adults, use lower doses, monitor sodium and falls risk, and avoid tricyclics. In bipolar depression, antidepressants may precipitate mania without a mood stabiliser.

## Key points

- Two weeks of low mood or anhedonia with additional symptoms defines a depressive episode; always exclude bipolar disorder and organic causes
- Psychological therapy first for less severe depression; combine CBT and an SSRI for more severe illness
- Sertraline is the SSRI of choice in cardiac disease and pregnancy; citalopram prolongs QT
- SSRIs cause hyponatraemia and bleeding, particularly in the elderly
- Continue treatment for at least 6 months after remission and taper slowly
- Serotonin syndrome presents with clonus and hyperreflexia within hours; NMS with rigidity over days

title: Schizophrenia and antipsychotic therapy
summary: Diagnostic features and prognostic factors in schizophrenia, the pharmacology and adverse effects of typical and atypical antipsychotics, clozapine monitoring and the management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
content:
## Overview

Schizophrenia affects about 1 percent of the population with onset typically between 15 and 35 years, earlier in men. It is a heterogeneous syndrome of positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganisation), negative symptoms (blunted affect, alogia, avolition, social withdrawal) and cognitive impairment. Physicians encounter it through antipsychotic side effects and the excess cardiometabolic mortality that shortens life expectancy by 15-20 years.

## Diagnosis

Schneider's first-rank symptoms: auditory hallucinations in the third person, running commentary or thought echo; thought insertion, withdrawal or broadcasting; delusions of control (passivity phenomena); delusional perception. ICD-11 requires at least two core symptoms (including one of delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder or passivity) for at least one month, without an organic or substance cause. Organic differentials include temporal lobe epilepsy, drug-induced psychosis (cannabis, amphetamines, steroids), delirium, autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA receptor), Huntington disease, Wilson disease, SLE and neurosyphilis; first presentation warrants physical examination, bloods, urine drug screen and, where indicated, neuroimaging.

Risk factors: family history (heritability around 80 percent), obstetric complications, urban birth, migration, childhood adversity, cannabis use in adolescence and advanced paternal age. Poor prognostic factors include insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, male sex, early onset, low IQ, social isolation, lack of an obvious precipitant and long duration of untreated psychosis.

## Management principles

NICE recommends early intervention in psychosis services, an oral antipsychotic chosen jointly with the patient after discussing side effect profiles, and CBT for psychosis plus family intervention for all. Assess baseline weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, ECG and physical activity, and monitor these at 12 weeks, one year and annually. Long-acting depot injections improve adherence. Clozapine is indicated after two adequate antipsychotic trials (at least one atypical) have failed.

## Antipsychotic classes

| Class | Examples | Profile |
|---|---|---|
| Typical (first generation) | Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, flupentixol, zuclopenthixol | Potent D2 antagonism; extrapyramidal side effects and hyperprolactinaemia dominate; chlorpromazine causes photosensitivity and sedation |
| Atypical (second generation) | Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, amisulpride, paliperidone, lurasidone | Serotonin 5-HT2A and D2 antagonism; fewer EPSE but more metabolic effects (olanzapine and clozapine worst); risperidone, amisulpride and paliperidone raise prolactin; aripiprazole is a partial agonist with the most benign metabolic and prolactin profile; quetiapine is sedating and hypotensive |
| Clozapine | | Most effective for treatment-resistant disease; agranulocytosis (mandatory FBC monitoring weekly for 18 weeks, fortnightly to a year, then monthly), myocarditis, seizures, hypersalivation, constipation that may cause fatal ileus, weight gain and diabetes; smoking cessation raises levels |

## Extrapyramidal side effects

- Acute dystonia: torticollis, oculogyric crisis within hours to days; treat with intramuscular procyclidine or benzatropine
- Akathisia: inner restlessness within weeks; reduce dose, propranolol or a benzodiazepine
- Parkinsonism: within weeks to months; reduce dose, switch agent, anticholinergic
- Tardive dyskinesia: orofacial choreoathetoid movements after months to years; often irreversible; withdraw or switch to clozapine; tetrabenazine or valbenazine

## Other adverse effects

Hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis), QT prolongation (haloperidol, pimozide, and to a lesser degree most agents; check ECG), postural hypotension, anticholinergic effects, sedation, reduced seizure threshold, venous thromboembolism, and increased stroke and mortality in older patients with dementia (avoid for behavioural symptoms unless severe distress or risk).

## Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

A rare, life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction developing over days: hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, autonomic instability, raised creatine kinase, leukocytosis, and acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis. Stop the antipsychotic, cool and hydrate, give benzodiazepines, and consider dantrolene or bromocriptine in intensive care. Reintroduce antipsychotics cautiously after two weeks with a different, lower-potency agent. Abrupt withdrawal of levodopa in Parkinson disease produces an identical picture.

## Key points

- Third-person auditory hallucinations, thought interference and passivity are first-rank symptoms
- Exclude organic and drug-induced psychosis at first presentation
- Atypical antipsychotics trade extrapyramidal effects for metabolic ones; monitor weight, glucose, lipids and ECG
- Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance and requires regular neutrophil monitoring
- Acute dystonia is treated with procyclidine; tardive dyskinesia may be irreversible
- Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with rigidity, hyperthermia and raised creatine kinase over days

title: Acute kidney injury
summary: KDIGO staging, pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal causes, initial assessment, nephrotoxic drug management, indications for renal replacement therapy and the treatment of hyperkalaemia.
content:
## Overview

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt decline in kidney function, complicating around 15 percent of hospital admissions and carrying a mortality above 20 percent. It is defined by KDIGO criteria: a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours.

| Stage | Creatinine | Urine output |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.5-1.9 times baseline or rise of 26 micromol/L or more | Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12 hours |
| 2 | 2.0-2.9 times baseline | Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more |
| 3 | 3 times baseline or more, or creatinine above 354 micromol/L, or renal replacement started | Below 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours or anuria for 12 hours |

## Causes

**Pre-renal (around 60 percent)**: reduced perfusion from hypovolaemia (haemorrhage, diarrhoea, vomiting, diuretics, burns), hypotension, sepsis, cardiac failure, hepatorenal syndrome, renal artery stenosis with ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs (afferent arteriolar constriction) and abdominal compartment syndrome. The tubules remain intact, so urine is concentrated (osmolality above 500, sodium below 20 mmol/L, fractional excretion of sodium below 1 percent) and function recovers rapidly with restoration of perfusion. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to acute tubular necrosis.

**Intrinsic renal (around 35 percent)**:
- Acute tubular necrosis: ischaemia or nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, haemoglobin, cisplatin, light chains in myeloma). Muddy brown granular casts, urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, isosthenuria
- Acute interstitial nephritis: drugs (NSAIDs, penicillins, proton pump inhibitors, allopurinol, rifampicin), infection, sarcoidosis, TINU; fever, rash, eosinophilia and sterile pyuria with white cell casts
- Glomerulonephritis and small vessel vasculitis: haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts, systemic features; rapidly progressive GN is a renal emergency requiring urgent immunology and biopsy
- Vascular: thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS, TTP), cholesterol emboli, malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis

**Post-renal (around 5 percent)**: obstruction from prostate enlargement, stones, tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis, blocked catheter or neurogenic bladder; complete anuria strongly suggests obstruction.

## Assessment

Take a careful history of fluid losses, drugs and urinary symptoms. Examine for volume status, palpable bladder and signs of systemic disease. Urinalysis is the single most useful bedside test: bland in pre-renal AKI and ATN; blood and protein in glomerulonephritis. Renal ultrasound within 24 hours (within 6 hours if pyonephrosis is suspected or there is no identifiable cause) excludes obstruction. Send urine protein-creatinine ratio, creatine kinase, ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complement, immunoglobulins and serum free light chains where the cause is unclear. Renal biopsy is indicated for suspected glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis or unexplained AKI without recovery.

## Management

- Treat the cause: fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid for hypovolaemia, relief of obstruction by catheter or nephrostomy, treatment of sepsis
- Stop nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (temporarily), diuretics if hypovolaemic. Hold metformin (lactic acidosis) and review lithium, digoxin, DOAC, opioid and gabapentinoid doses
- Monitor fluid balance, daily weights, electrolytes and acid-base status
- Avoid contrast where possible; volume expansion is the only proven preventive measure

## Indications for renal replacement therapy

Refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory pulmonary oedema, severe metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.15), uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy) and certain poisonings. Continuous veno-venous haemofiltration is favoured in haemodynamically unstable patients.

## Hyperkalaemia

Above 6.5 mmol/L or with ECG changes (tall tented T waves, flattened P waves, broad QRS, sine wave): 10 mL of 10 percent calcium chloride or 30 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate intravenously for membrane stabilisation, then 10 units of soluble insulin in 25 g glucose, nebulised salbutamol, and treat the cause. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer for ongoing potassium removal; dialysis if refractory.

## Key points

- Creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L in 48 hours, 1.5 times baseline in 7 days, or oliguria below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours defines AKI
- Urinalysis and ultrasound within 24 hours are essential first investigations
- Concentrated urine with low sodium suggests pre-renal AKI; muddy brown casts suggest ATN; blood and protein suggest glomerular disease
- Stop NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and metformin; adjust renally cleared drugs
- Renal replacement is for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload and uraemic complications
- Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes needs intravenous calcium first, then insulin-glucose

title: Glomerulonephritis and the nephrotic syndrome
summary: Distinguishing nephritic and nephrotic presentations, the major primary and secondary glomerular diseases with their histology, serology and associations, and principles of treatment.
content:
## Overview

Glomerular disease presents along a spectrum from asymptomatic haematuria or proteinuria through nephritic and nephrotic syndromes to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Part 1 questions match a clinical vignette to a histological diagnosis using age, associations, serology, complement levels and biopsy appearances.

## Nephrotic versus nephritic syndrome

| Feature | Nephrotic | Nephritic |
|---|---|---|
| Proteinuria | Above 3.5 g/24 h (uPCR above 300 mg/mmol) | Mild to moderate |
| Haematuria | Absent or microscopic | Present, red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells |
| Oedema | Marked | Variable |
| Albumin | Below 30 g/L | Normal or mildly low |
| Blood pressure | Normal or raised | Raised |
| GFR | Usually preserved initially | Reduced, often acutely |
| Complications | Thrombosis, infection, hyperlipidaemia | Acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema |

Nephrotic complications: hypercoagulability from urinary loss of antithrombin III (renal vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism), infection from immunoglobulin loss, and hypercholesterolaemia.

## Primary glomerular diseases

**Minimal change disease**: the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and 10-25 percent in adults. Normal light microscopy; podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy. Associated with NSAIDs, Hodgkin lymphoma and atopy. Highly selective proteinuria. Over 90 percent respond to prednisolone; relapses are common and calcineurin inhibitors, rituximab or cyclophosphamide are used for frequent relapse.

**Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis**: commonest primary nephrotic cause in Black adults. Secondary forms with HIV (collapsing variant), heroin, obesity, sickle cell disease, reflux nephropathy and APOL1 variants. Steroid response is partial; progression to end-stage disease is common and recurrence after transplantation occurs in 30-50 percent.

**Membranous nephropathy**: the commonest primary nephrotic cause in white adults. Subepithelial immune deposits with spikes on silver stain. Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies in 70-80 percent of primary cases. Secondary causes include malignancy (lung, colon, breast), hepatitis B, SLE (class V), gold, penicillamine and NSAIDs. Treat with renin-angiotensin blockade for 6 months; rituximab or cyclophosphamide-steroid regimens for high-risk disease.

**IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)**: the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Visible haematuria 1-2 days after an upper respiratory infection in a young adult, or asymptomatic microscopic haematuria with proteinuria. Mesangial IgA deposits; normal complement. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the systemic form with purpura, arthralgia and abdominal pain. Treat with ACE inhibitor or ARB, SGLT2 inhibitor, blood pressure control; steroids or targeted-release budesonide for persistent proteinuria above 1 g daily.

**Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**: nephritic syndrome 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after impetigo, typically in children. Low C3, raised anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B, subepithelial humps. Supportive treatment with an excellent prognosis.

**Membranoproliferative GN**: low complement, tram-track appearance; associated with hepatitis C and cryoglobulinaemia; C3 glomerulopathy involves alternative complement dysregulation.

## Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

Crescents on biopsy with kidney function declining over days to weeks. Three immunofluorescence patterns:
- Linear IgG: anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture), with pulmonary haemorrhage in smokers; treat with plasma exchange, cyclophosphamide and steroids
- Pauci-immune: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, PR3-ANCA; microscopic polyangiitis, MPO-ANCA); rituximab or cyclophosphamide with steroids, avacopan as steroid-sparing
- Granular immune complex: lupus nephritis (class IV), post-infectious, IgA, cryoglobulinaemia

## Secondary glomerular disease

Diabetic nephropathy (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, the commonest cause of end-stage disease), lupus nephritis (low complement, anti-dsDNA; mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide with steroids), amyloidosis (Congo red apple-green birefringence), Alport syndrome (X-linked collagen IV, sensorineural deafness).

## Complement patterns

Low C3 and C4: SLE, cryoglobulinaemia, endocarditis. Low C3 with normal C4: post-streptococcal GN, C3 glomerulopathy. Normal complement: IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, minimal change, FSGS, membranous.

## Key points

- Nephrotic syndrome is proteinuria above 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; nephritic syndrome features haematuria, hypertension and falling GFR
- Minimal change in children, membranous in white adults, FSGS in Black adults are the leading nephrotic causes
- IgA nephropathy is the commonest glomerulonephritis and follows upper respiratory infection within days; post-streptococcal GN follows after weeks and has low C3
- Anti-PLA2R antibodies indicate primary membranous nephropathy; screen for malignancy in secondary disease
- Crescentic GN with linear IgG is anti-GBM disease; pauci-immune crescentic GN is ANCA vasculitis
- ACE inhibitors or ARBs and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce proteinuria in all proteinuric glomerular disease

title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
summary: Diagnosis and severity grading, the NICE inhaled therapy pathway, exacerbation management, indications for long-term oxygen, non-invasive ventilation and other interventions that alter prognosis.
content:
## Overview

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a preventable, progressive condition of persistent airflow obstruction caused by a mixture of small airway disease (chronic bronchitis) and parenchymal destruction (emphysema), overwhelmingly due to tobacco smoke in the UK. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency should be considered in patients under 45, non-smokers and those with basal emphysema.

## Diagnosis and severity

Consider COPD in anyone over 35 with a risk factor and exertional breathlessness, chronic cough, regular sputum production or frequent winter bronchitis. Diagnosis requires post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC below 0.7. Severity by FEV1 percent predicted:

| Stage | FEV1 percent predicted |
|---|---|
| 1 Mild | 80 or above (symptoms must be present) |
| 2 Moderate | 50-79 |
| 3 Severe | 30-49 |
| 4 Very severe | Below 30 |

Symptom burden is graded by the MRC dyspnoea scale (1-5) and the CAT score. Baseline investigations: chest X-ray, full blood count, BMI, and consider alpha-1 antitrypsin, CT and echocardiography. Asthmatic features: previous asthma or atopy, eosinophils above 300 cells/microlitre, FEV1 variation over 400 mL or diurnal peak flow variation of at least 20 percent.

## Non-pharmacological management

Smoking cessation is the only intervention besides oxygen and lung volume reduction that improves survival; offer varenicline, nicotine replacement or bupropion with behavioural support. Pulmonary rehabilitation for anyone with MRC grade 3 or above or a recent exacerbation improves exercise capacity and quality of life. Annual influenza and one-off pneumococcal vaccination, plus COVID-19 and RSV vaccines as eligible.

## Inhaled therapy (NICE 2019)

1. Short-acting beta-agonist or short-acting muscarinic antagonist as required for all
2. If still limited by symptoms or exacerbations, with no asthmatic features: long-acting beta-agonist plus long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LABA + LAMA)
3. With asthmatic features or steroid responsiveness: LABA plus inhaled corticosteroid (LABA + ICS)
4. Escalate to triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) if a severe exacerbation or two moderate exacerbations occur within a year on dual therapy, or if day-to-day symptoms persist on LABA + ICS. Review after 3 months if started for symptoms alone and step down if no benefit

Inhaled corticosteroids increase pneumonia risk; eosinophil count predicts benefit.

## Oral therapies

- Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) for severe disease with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations despite triple therapy
- Azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly for non-smokers with frequent exacerbations after excluding QT prolongation, hearing loss and atypical mycobacteria
- Carbocisteine for chronic productive cough; standby rescue pack of prednisolone and antibiotics for self-management

## Long-term oxygen therapy

Assess with two arterial blood gases at least 3 weeks apart in stable patients with FEV1 below 30 percent, cyanosis, polycythaemia, peripheral oedema, raised JVP or saturations at or below 92 percent. Offer LTOT for at least 15 hours daily if PaO2 is below 7.3 kPa, or 7.3-8 kPa with polycythaemia, nocturnal hypoxaemia, peripheral oedema or pulmonary hypertension. Do not offer to current smokers or those who continue to smoke.

## Exacerbations

Increase in breathlessness, sputum volume or purulence beyond normal variation. Around half are infective (Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, viruses). Treatment: controlled oxygen via Venturi mask targeting saturations 88-92 percent until blood gases exclude hypercapnia, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, and antibiotics (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin) if sputum is purulent or there are signs of pneumonia. Non-invasive ventilation for persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH 7.25-7.35 after one hour of optimal medical treatment; consider invasive ventilation below 7.25. Lung volume reduction surgery or endobronchial valves are options for heterogeneous upper lobe emphysema.

## Key points

- Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms obstruction; grade severity by FEV1 percent predicted
- Smoking cessation is the most important intervention and one of the few that improves survival
- LABA + LAMA is the second step unless asthmatic features favour LABA + ICS; escalate to triple therapy for exacerbations
- LTOT when PaO2 is below 7.3 kPa (or 7.3-8 kPa with complications) for at least 15 hours daily, never in current smokers
- In exacerbations target saturations 88-92 percent and use NIV when pH is 7.25-7.35 after initial treatment
- Prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days; antibiotics only if sputum is purulent

title: Interstitial lung disease
summary: Classification of diffuse parenchymal lung disease, the clinical and radiological features of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis and drug- and connective tissue-related fibrosis, and the role of antifibrotic therapy.
content:
## Overview

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) describes a heterogeneous group of more than 200 disorders that inflame or scar the pulmonary parenchyma. They share exertional breathlessness, dry cough, fine bibasal inspiratory crackles, restrictive spirometry with reduced gas transfer, and reticular or ground-glass change on high-resolution CT. Correct classification matters because immunosuppression helps some and harms others.

## Classification

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias | Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (usual interstitial pneumonia pattern), non-specific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, acute interstitial pneumonia |
| Known cause or association | Connective tissue disease (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, myositis, Sjogren), drugs, occupational (asbestosis, silicosis, coal worker pneumoconiosis), hypersensitivity pneumonitis, radiation |
| Granulomatous | Sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, berylliosis |
| Other | Lymphangioleiomyomatosis, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, eosinophilic pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis |

Upper zone predominance: coal worker pneumoconiosis, histiocytosis, ankylosing spondylitis, radiation, sarcoidosis, silicosis, tuberculosis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, berylliosis. Lower zone predominance: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, asbestosis, connective tissue disease (except ankylosing spondylitis), drug-induced.

## Investigations

Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern (FEV1/FVC normal or raised, FVC reduced) with reduced total lung capacity and reduced transfer factor (TLCO). High-resolution CT is the key investigation; a confident UIP pattern (basal, subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, without extensive ground glass) avoids the need for biopsy. Bloods: autoimmune serology (ANA, ENA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, myositis panel, anti-Scl70), avian and fungal precipitins, ACE and calcium in sarcoidosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage lymphocytosis supports hypersensitivity pneumonitis or sarcoidosis. Surgical or cryobiopsy is reserved for indeterminate cases after multidisciplinary discussion.

## Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The commonest idiopathic ILD, affecting men over 60 with a history of smoking. Progressive breathlessness over months, clubbing in 50 percent, fine velcro crackles. Median survival is 3-4 years. Antifibrotic therapy with pirfenidone (photosensitivity, gastrointestinal upset, hepatotoxicity) or nintedanib (diarrhoea, hepatotoxicity, bleeding risk) slows the decline in FVC and is offered when FVC is 50-80 percent predicted; treatment is stopped if FVC falls 10 percent or more in 12 months. Steroids and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (PANTHER trial). Manage cough and reflux, offer pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen and early palliative care, and refer for transplantation where appropriate.

## Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Immune response to inhaled organic antigens: bird fancier's lung (avian proteins), farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay), malt worker's lung (Aspergillus clavatus), humidifier lung, hot tub lung (Mycobacterium avium). Acute disease produces fever, cough and breathlessness 4-8 hours after exposure with resolution over days; chronic disease causes insidious fibrosis. CT shows centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation and, in chronic disease, upper zone fibrosis. Treatment is antigen avoidance and corticosteroids.

## Sarcoidosis

A multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown cause, commoner in young adults and in Black populations. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, anterior uveitis, lupus pernio, arthralgia, hypercalcaemia (vitamin D activation by macrophages), cranial nerve palsies and cardiac conduction disease. Lofgren syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthralgia) has an excellent prognosis. Raised ACE is supportive but not diagnostic. Stage by chest X-ray from 0 (normal) to 4 (fibrosis). Most stage 1 disease resolves spontaneously; steroids are indicated for parenchymal disease with symptoms or declining function, hypercalcaemia, and eye, cardiac or neurological involvement, with methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent.

## Drug-induced and connective tissue-related ILD

Drugs: amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin, busulfan, cyclophosphamide, gold, sulfasalazine, immune checkpoint inhibitors. Systemic sclerosis (anti-Scl70) causes NSIP-pattern fibrosis treated with mycophenolate, nintedanib or tocilizumab. Rheumatoid arthritis produces UIP or NSIP in around 10 percent, with additional risks from methotrexate and rheumatoid nodules. Asbestosis follows heavy exposure with a 20-40 year latency and increases the risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma; pleural plaques alone are benign.

## Key points

- Restrictive spirometry with reduced TLCO and bibasal velcro crackles suggest ILD; HRCT is the key investigation
- A UIP pattern on HRCT in an older smoker allows diagnosis of IPF without biopsy
- Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow IPF when FVC is 50-80 percent; steroids are harmful in IPF
- Upper zone fibrosis: sarcoidosis, silicosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, ankylosing spondylitis; lower zone: IPF, asbestosis, connective tissue disease
- Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with erythema nodosum and arthralgia is Lofgren syndrome and usually self-limits
- Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin and bleomycin are the classic pulmonary fibrosis drugs

title: Rheumatoid arthritis
summary: Diagnosis using the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria, serology, extra-articular disease, treat-to-target DMARD strategy, biologic selection and the monitoring requirements of methotrexate and related drugs.
content:
## Overview

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis affecting around 1 percent of adults, women two to three times more often than men, with peak onset between 40 and 60. Synovial inflammation driven by TNF-alpha, IL-6 and autoreactive T and B cells produces pannus that erodes cartilage and bone. Early aggressive treatment within a window of opportunity prevents irreversible joint damage.

## Clinical features

Insidious onset of pain, swelling and morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes in the small joints of the hands (metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal), wrists and feet (metatarsophalangeal), with sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints. Later deformities include ulnar deviation, swan neck and boutonniere deformities, Z-thumb, and atlanto-axial subluxation (screen with cervical spine flexion-extension views before anaesthesia).

## Diagnosis

The 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria score joint involvement (0-5), serology (0-3), acute phase reactants (0-1) and symptom duration over 6 weeks (0-1); a total of 6 or more out of 10 classifies RA.

| Test | Notes |
|---|---|
| Rheumatoid factor | IgM against Fc portion of IgG; positive in 70 percent but also in Sjogren, SLE, hepatitis C, endocarditis, elderly |
| Anti-CCP antibodies | Similar sensitivity, specificity above 95 percent; predicts erosive disease; may precede symptoms by years |
| ESR and CRP | Raised; used in disease activity scores |
| X-rays | Periarticular osteopenia, soft tissue swelling, joint space loss, marginal erosions; ultrasound or MRI detects early synovitis |
| FBC | Normocytic anaemia of chronic disease; thrombocytosis |

Poor prognostic factors: anti-CCP positivity, high RF titre, early erosions, extra-articular disease, HLA-DR4 shared epitope, female sex, insidious onset and smoking.

## Extra-articular manifestations

- Ocular: keratoconjunctivitis sicca (commonest), episcleritis, scleritis, scleromalacia perforans, corneal ulceration
- Pulmonary: pleural effusion (low glucose), interstitial lung disease, rheumatoid nodules, Caplan syndrome (with pneumoconiosis), bronchiectasis, methotrexate pneumonitis
- Cardiac: pericarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis (RA doubles cardiovascular risk)
- Haematological: Felty syndrome (RA, splenomegaly, neutropenia), anaemia
