- Neurological: carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical myelopathy, mononeuritis multiplex
- Skin: rheumatoid nodules (RF positive), vasculitic ulcers, pyoderma gangrenosum
- Renal: AA amyloidosis, drug nephrotoxicity
- Osteoporosis, depression and increased lymphoma risk

## Management

Treat to target of remission or low disease activity using the DAS28, reviewing monthly until achieved. Start conventional synthetic DMARD monotherapy within 3 months of persistent symptoms: methotrexate is first choice (oral or subcutaneous, weekly, with folic acid on a different day), with leflunomide or sulfasalazine as alternatives; hydroxychloroquine for mild palindromic disease. Bridge with short-course oral, intramuscular or intra-articular glucocorticoids. Escalate to combination DMARDs if the target is not met.

Biologic or targeted synthetic therapy is offered when DAS28 exceeds 5.1 (or 3.2 in some NICE pathways) despite two conventional DMARDs including methotrexate, usually alongside methotrexate:

- TNF inhibitors: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab
- IL-6 receptor blockade: tocilizumab, sarilumab
- B-cell depletion: rituximab (after TNF inhibitor failure)
- T-cell co-stimulation blockade: abatacept
- JAK inhibitors: tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib (oral; increased risk of VTE, major cardiovascular events and malignancy in over-65s and smokers, so used cautiously)

Screen for tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C and HIV before biologics. Manage cardiovascular risk, bone health, vaccination (avoid live vaccines on biologics) and refer for physiotherapy, occupational therapy and podiatry.

## Methotrexate monitoring and toxicity

FBC, LFTs and renal function every 2 weeks until dose stable, then monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months. Adverse effects: mucositis, marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis (dry cough and breathlessness, stop drug), teratogenicity (contraception for at least 6 months after stopping in either partner). Avoid trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (fatal pancytopenia) and limit alcohol. Folinic acid rescue for overdose. Hydroxychloroquine requires retinal screening; sulfasalazine causes oligospermia.

## Key points

- Symmetrical small joint synovitis with morning stiffness over 30 minutes and DIP sparing suggests RA; refer urgently without waiting for bloods
- Anti-CCP is highly specific and predicts erosive disease
- Start methotrexate within 3 months of symptom onset and treat to a DAS28 target
- Biologics follow failure of two conventional DMARDs; screen for TB and hepatitis first
- Never combine methotrexate with trimethoprim; monitor FBC, LFTs and renal function regularly
- RA doubles cardiovascular risk and causes keratoconjunctivitis sicca, ILD and Felty syndrome

title: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
summary: Pathophysiology, risk factors and triggers of gout, diagnosis by crystal identification, acute and urate-lowering treatment with UK targets, and the features that distinguish calcium pyrophosphate deposition.
content:
## Overview

Gout is the commonest inflammatory arthritis in men and in older women, affecting around 2.5 percent of UK adults. It results from monosodium urate crystal deposition when serum urate exceeds its solubility limit of about 360-400 micromol/L. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD, previously pseudogout) produces a similar acute arthritis in older adults but with different crystals, associations and treatment.

## Pathophysiology and risk factors

Hyperuricaemia arises from underexcretion (90 percent) or overproduction. Risk factors: male sex, age, obesity, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, diuretics (thiazides and loop), low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, alcohol (especially beer), red meat, seafood and fructose-sweetened drinks. Overproduction occurs with myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, psoriasis, tumour lysis, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HPRT deficiency) and glycogen storage disease.

## Clinical features

Acute gout presents with an abrupt, exquisitely painful, red, swollen joint, classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) but also the midfoot, ankle, knee, wrist, fingers and elbow. Attacks peak within 24 hours and resolve over 1-2 weeks, often triggered by dehydration, surgery, illness, dietary excess or starting urate-lowering therapy. Chronic tophaceous gout produces firm white subcutaneous deposits on the ear helix, fingers, elbows and Achilles tendon, and destructive polyarthritis. Urate nephrolithiasis and chronic urate nephropathy are renal complications.

## Diagnosis

Joint aspiration with polarised light microscopy is definitive: monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent. Aspirate also excludes septic arthritis, which can coexist. Serum urate may be normal during an acute attack, so measure it at least 2 weeks after the flare has settled. X-rays show punched-out juxta-articular erosions with overhanging edges and preserved joint space in chronic disease; ultrasound shows a double contour sign and dual-energy CT visualises urate deposits.

## Acute treatment

- First line: NSAID at full dose with a proton pump inhibitor, or oral colchicine 500 micrograms two to four times daily (limit to 500 micrograms twice daily in renal impairment or with statins or CYP3A4 inhibitors; diarrhoea limits use); choice depends on comorbidity
- Corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 30-35 mg for 5 days, or intra-articular or intramuscular) when NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated, for example in CKD
- IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) for refractory flares
- Continue established urate-lowering therapy during a flare; rest, ice and analgesia

## Urate-lowering therapy

NICE 2022 recommends offering ULT after a first attack in patients with two or more flares a year, tophi, chronic gouty arthritis, joint damage, CKD stage 3 or worse, diuretic use or a very high urate, and discussing it with everyone after a first flare. Start 2-4 weeks after the flare settles and titrate to a serum urate target below 360 micromol/L, or below 300 micromol/L if tophi or frequent flares are present.

| Drug | Notes |
|---|---|
| Allopurinol | First line xanthine oxidase inhibitor; start 100 mg daily (50 mg in CKD) and increase monthly; hypersensitivity syndrome risk with HLA-B*58:01 (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai); interacts with azathioprine and mercaptopurine (reduce to a quarter dose or avoid) |
| Febuxostat | Alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor when allopurinol is not tolerated or ineffective; MHRA warning in established cardiovascular disease |

Flare prophylaxis with colchicine 500 micrograms once or twice daily (or a low-dose NSAID) for up to 6 months when starting or up-titrating ULT. Avoid thiazides where possible.

## Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

Acute CPP crystal arthritis affects older adults, most often the knee, wrist or shoulder, sometimes after illness or surgery. Crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent. X-rays show chondrocalcinosis (linear calcification of menisci and triangular fibrocartilage). Associated with hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphatasia and Wilson disease; screen younger patients or those with polyarticular disease. Treatment is aspiration, intra-articular steroid, NSAIDs or colchicine; there is no crystal-lowering therapy.

## Key points

- Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals confirm gout; rhomboid, weakly positive crystals indicate CPPD
- Serum urate may be normal during a flare; measure 2 weeks after resolution
- NSAIDs or colchicine first line for acute gout; steroids when both are contraindicated
- Start allopurinol 2-4 weeks after a flare with colchicine cover, and titrate to urate below 360 micromol/L (300 with tophi)
- Allopurinol with azathioprine risks fatal marrow suppression; HLA-B*58:01 predicts hypersensitivity
- Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray and associations with hyperparathyroidism and haemochromatosis point to CPPD
